reason: A thoughtful take on how AI makes personal, single-user software practical.
content_html:
Some of the most useful software I own has exactly one user.

Me.

Lately, I’ve been building little applications with artificial intelligence to solve particular problems unique to me. It’s an expansion on the automation I’ve done my whole life, but now "build an app" is a legitimate tool next to "build a script." The more of these I make, the more I appreciate the possibilities of software built for an audience of one.

For example, I’ve built an application that turns my Apple TV into a custom status board. It shows my calendar, local weather, camera views, and other information I want to see. I get to decide what belongs on that screen because I’m the person looking at it.

Yesterday I got thinking it would be nice for my status board app to have a linear calendar (where each month gets its own row) for the year showing major events. After three prompts I had it working. But it was showing the calendar year. I wanted it to start with the current month and show the next 12 months. That took another prompt.

I’ve also built an application that drives my Vestaboard with custom postings. On my Mac, I’ve made an application that lets me interact with my Obsidian data in ways Obsidian itself doesn’t offer. I’ve built several Obsidian plugins, too.

These are small, specific projects, and I use them. That feels like a pretty good definition of success.

Building for myself makes a lot of the decisions easy. I already know which Mac this will run on and how my data is organized. When I’m deciding what a button should do, I can work from the way I actually use the computer.

The software only has to work on my systems. Supporting every possible configuration can stay off the list. When I need a feature, I can work on adding it. When something doesn’t matter to me, I can leave it out.

That limited scope helps enormously. As I get better at explaining what I want, I’m finding that AI does a remarkably good job of helping me put these little systems together.

Of course, I still have to test what the AI builds. Getting an app to launch doesn’t tell me whether it handles my data properly, and I’m responsible for what I run on my computers. But now, when I think, "I wish my computer could do this," building it myself is an option.

I’m hearing about all sorts of these projects in the Robot Builders Club. People who haven’t developed software before are making apps for themselves. They can explain the problem they want to solve because it’s something they already deal with.

And they have a good way to judge the result. Does the app do the thing they wanted it to do? They can try it in their own work and find out.

Then there’s the question of selling what you’ve made.

My inbox is filling up with pitches from people building productivity apps. I understand the enthusiasm. Once you’ve made something useful, it’s easy to start thinking about who else might want it.

But I’m reluctant to recommend an app when I don’t know whether the developer will still be working on it a year from now. What happens when an operating system update breaks something? I want to have some confidence that readers will get help, especially if they’re trusting the app with their work.

Selling it means taking responsibility for other people’s use of it. If you’re excited about that work too, great. It’s worth asking yourself before you put a price on the download.

If your app makes a daily task easier, you already have a reason to keep using it. You can change it when your needs change and spend as much time on it as you like. The fact that someone else might never want it (or you’re not interested in the extra burden that comes with distributing it) doesn’t make it any less useful to you.

I like that I can decide my calendar should start with the current month and then make it work that way. Someone else might prefer January at the top. Mine suits me.

Start with something small enough that you can explain what you want it to do.

What’s one small thing you wish your computer did just for you?

An audience of one is enough.

The post An Audience of One Is Enough appeared first on MacSparky.

title: Start
summary: The cultural impresario has always had leverage. Invest time and money and put on a show. Start a cable network, a book publishing company or become a concert promoter. You’re the gatekeeper, an adjudicator of status, a person who can transform people’s lives simply by amplifying and spreading ideas and allowing art to reach its […]
reason: Seth Godin on why anyone can now be the one who starts something.
content_html:
The cultural impresario has always had leverage.

Invest time and money and put on a show. Start a cable network, a book publishing company or become a concert promoter. You’re the gatekeeper, an adjudicator of status, a person who can transform people’s lives simply by amplifying and spreading ideas and allowing art to reach its audience.

Time and money were apparently the gating factors. It takes a while to turn a profit, and it’s uncertain and hard work.

Except…

New platforms and tools remove both time and money as barriers.

Penn and Teller needed their fame and the CW network to launch their cable show Fool Us. But now, anyone can start a competitor on YouTube in a weekend.

A radio pundit needed to spend years to build a syndicated network of terrestrial stations, but now you can start a podcast, in your basement, for free. In a weekend.

Gallerists don’t need galleries, and you don’t even need a building to coordinate a foster-home-based pet shelter.

So what’s the impediment?

I’m guessing that if you got the call today, you could put together your ideas for a book, or five minutes of standup or even the software you’d code.

But we don’t need the specific call. We’ve all been called.

The barrier is simple: fear. The fear of beginning and of sticking with it. The fear of succeeding (or failing). The fear of impostor syndrome. And the fear of going forward without a guarantee.

So let’s call it that. Fear is real, but fear might not be rational.

Begin.

title: Why are we all worked up about atomicity when applying hot-patches if we can just suspend all the threads?
summary: Suspending all the threads stops the threads that are there now, those are not the only possible sources of change. The post Why are we all worked up about atomicity when applying hot-patches if we can just suspend all the threads? appeared first on The Old New Thing .
reason: Raymond Chen on why hot-patching needs atomicity, a classic Windows engineering lesson.
content_html:
I noted that one of the concerns of the Windows hot-patching system is that the patch can be activated atomically. But why does it need to be atomic? Can’t just suspend all the threads of the process (except for the one doing the patching)? That way, nobody else can be executing a half-installed patch.

For processors with variable-length instructions (looking at you, x86), the patched instruction cannot be shorter than its replacement. This applies even if you can suspend all the threads of the process, because you might suspend a thread just as it’s about to execute bytes from what would be the second of half of the replacement instruction.

instruction
pointer
    ↓
original XX YY
 
patch AA BB

If you were unlucky and froze the thread after it executed the XX instruction and was about to execute the YY instruction, and then replaced both bytes with a two-byte instruction AA BB, then when the thread resumes, it will execute BB as if it were the start of a new instruction.

Okay fine, so we’ll make sure that the original instruction is at least as big as the replacement instruction, so that a frozen thread is never caught in the middle of the replacement instruction. But assuming we do that, can’t we just suspend all the threads, and then patch at will without having to worry about atomicity?

While it’s true that you suspended all the threads in the process, that doesn’t prevent new threads from being created in the process by a function like Create­Remote­Thread. The caller of Create­Remote­Thread can specify whether the new thread is suspended or not, and if it chooses non-suspended (or if it chose suspended and then decided to resume it), you now have a live thread running in the process while you are busy trying to patch it.

Atomicity is important so that you don’t accidentally patch code while an injected thread happens to be running it.

Bonus chatter: Now, atomicity is still not bulletproof, because even if you manage to suspend all the threads, and prevent new ones from being injected, you still have the case where somebody calls Write­Process­Memory to modify the bytes of the process while everything in it is suspended.

And we saw earlier that Write­Process­Memory is not atomic, so it’s possible that a two-byte Write­Process­Memory writes the first byte, and then you do your atomic update of both bytes, and then the Write­Process­Memory finishes by writing the second byte, leaving a mishmash of your patch and the rogue one.

On the other hand, anybody who was using Write­Process­Memory to do code patching was already broken because of this lack of atomicity, so we are not introducing a new problem.

Furthermore, since the hot-patching space is reserved for Windows Update, an outsider that uses Write­Process­Memory to apply a hot-patch from another process is already breaking the rules. At this point Windows Update says, “Look, I can’t protect myself from this, and you’re in double-unsupported territory by the time we got here, so whatever happens is your problem.”

The post Why are we all worked up about atomicity when applying hot-patches if we can just suspend all the threads? appeared first on The Old New Thing.

title: Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers
summary: Anthropic is using AI to build more powerful AI. And it appears to be working remarkably well, with the company's models improving roughly twice as quickly as a year ago, with little indication of slowing down. That's according to a new report published Thursday by the AI safety research organization METR, following an 11-week investigation […]
reason: Report that AI is speeding up AI development itself, a big shift in how software is built.
content_html:
Anthropic is using AI to build more powerful AI. And it appears to be working remarkably well, with the company’s models improving roughly twice as quickly as a year ago, with little indication of slowing down.

Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers

AI is dramatically speeding up Anthropic’s research, even as the company calls for slowing down AI development.

Inside Anthropic Headquarters As It’s Testing A Different Version Of Leadership

Inside Anthropic Headquarters As It’s Testing A Different Version Of Leadership

That’s according to a new report published Thursday by the AI safety research organization METR, following an 11-week investigation inside the company, as part of a report evaluating its AI research and development. The probe is separate from a program offering safety researchers “employee-like” access to systems in the wake of high-profile hacking incidents over the summer.

The findings offer some of the clearest evidence yet of AI accelerating its own development, raising questions about how quickly the technology could advance toward a future in which AI systems can improve themselves with little or no human involvement. They also come at a pivotal time for Anthropic, which is preparing to go public even as its CEO, Dario Amodei, has publicly called for labs to pump the brakes on AI development.

But while the report offers a rare glimpse into the inner workings of the world’s leading AI labs, what it leaves out is just as revealing. Anthropic was permitted to redact portions of the final report as part of its agreement with METR, and it appears to have exercised that power liberally, raising questions about how much the public really knows about the pace — and risks — of frontier AI development.

Here are some of the biggest takeaways.

AI is dramatically accelerating Anthropic’s research and development

One of METR’s most noteworthy findings is that Anthropic’s AI models are improving roughly twice as quickly as they were a year ago, with benchmark scores suggesting “that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year.” Crucially, METR’s researchers said they “are confident” that the acceleration was not simply due to scaling up the computing power used to train the models, which historically has been a major driver of AI progress.

Instead, the researchers said that the majority of the acceleration as of October “is due to AI,” with its contribution growing over time. That finding was supported by informal Slack polls and interviews with Anthropic employees, which pointed to sizable productivity gains. METR wrote that employees using Anthropic’s most capable internal model on average self-reported being around 12 times as productive at their respective work as they would have been without AI assistance, around double what staff had reported just a few months earlier while using Mythos 5.

METR’s report includes this graphic showing Anthropic employees’ responses to Slack polls about AI speeding up their work.

For now, much of that acceleration appears to be coming from AI assisting human researchers, rather than AI working independently, though METR warned that “there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon.” Notably, the researchers said they found no clear signs of diminishing returns or observable bottlenecks that could prevent “even faster acceleration.”

Three of Anthropic’s newest AI models remain under wraps

Anthropic’s researchers are using more advanced AI models than the rest of us, with a lot of the acceleration and productivity gains described by METR attributable to unreleased internal models.

Over the past six months, Anthropic has finished training three models it has yet to release, according to METR. The pace of development is swift, with the models — codenamed Model 2, Model 3, and Model 4 — completing training in July, August-September, and September-October, respectively. METR also identified an unreleased model dating back to 2022, called Unreleased 2022. “These are the codenames shared with us; we understand they have different internal codenames,” the researchers wrote.

Anthropic is keeping key information secret

Anthropic gave METR access to a host of non-public information, including confidential research, model performance data, and employee interviews as part of the research process. It had no obligation to do so and by METR’s own admission, the AI lab “shared more information than was initially scoped for this project, surpassing our expectations.” This is commendable, but it is worth noting that Anthropic did not grant researchers unrestricted access, nor the kind of “employee-like” access it has promised other METR safety researchers as part of a separate program announced last month. It is an important distinction, given the reputational benefits companies can gain from independent assessments, even when they come with significant restrictions.

And there were significant restrictions. Anthropic had the power to redact information from METR’s final report — and it used that power extensively. “We submitted a ~100-page full report on our assessment to Anthropic. For the public version, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative,” METR wrote on X.

METR reiterated those concerns throughout the report, highlighting other limitations on its access. “Our pipeline of information was relatively narrow, and a small number of our requests for data were denied.”

METR repeatedly stressed the impact Anthropic’s redaction decisions had on its ability to communicate its findings and for others to assess what’s going on at the company. It noted that much of the redacted evidence could have “multiple plausible interpretations,” making it difficult for the public to assess its findings, understand the uncertainties surrounding them, and judge the evidence themselves. “As a consequence [of the redactions], the public has to rely on METR’s judgment much more than would be ideal, given the weight of the questions answered here,” the report said.

In the report, METR said Anthropic justified the redactions on the grounds that releasing the information could benefit its rivals. However, METR said “most of the redacted information was very high-level,” even though it said it was not in position to comment whether redactions were justified commercially or not.

“We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work,” Anthropic cofounder Sam McCandlish acknowledged in a lengthy post on X responding to METR’s findings. “But we determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster,” he said, adding that doing so would make the risks METR is concerned about “worse.”

McCandlish said that it’s a trade-off, but maintained Anthropic had made the “right call” in deciding to redact the information. He said the company plans to publish its own report on the speed of AI progress “in the coming weeks,” as well as new steps it’s taking to strengthen safety.

Anthropic is accelerating the very technology it warns is dangerous and faster than many expected

The publication of METR’s report has provoked a fierce backlash among AI safety researchers and commentators, largely centered on an apparent contradiction at the heart of Anthropic’s approach to AI: The company has been one of the most outspoken advocates for safety and responsible development, yet the report suggests it is helping accelerate the technology toward a threshold many consider dangerous, while seemingly failing to live up to its own commitments to transparency and accountability.

For some, the findings suggest that even many of the field’s most aggressive predictions about AI progress may be too conservative. They indicate that recursive self-improvement — AI systems that can autonomously develop increasingly powerful successor systems without human intervention, potentially accelerating development dramatically — may be closer than previously thought, raising concerns about whether existing safety measures can keep pace. While METR’s report only covers Anthropic, OpenAI said in September that it is “making strong progress” toward building an AI researcher that can “further progress on deep learning and alignment” by March 2028.

The report provides evidence about just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development

Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and founder of Apollo Research, which conducts AI safety testing for several leading AI labs, told The Verge the report suggests a pace of AI-enabled research and development even faster than what was forecast in AI 2027, an influential scenario that envisions a key breakthrough toward self-improvement in early 2027. He said the report has attracted so much attention because it provides evidence about something that has been very hard to pin down: Just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development.

Hobbhahn said the findings were broadly in line with what many in the field had expected, perhaps a little faster. Alan Chan, a senior research fellow at tech policy research center GovAI, told The Verge that the findings should prompt skeptics to reconsider their stance on AI accelerating AI development, and possibly shorten their timelines to when we will have systems that can fully automate tasks like software engineering.

On X, other researchers commented on the rate of acceleration and its implications for AI development. Sydney Von Arx, founder and CEO of AI safety organization The Nightingale Collective and a former METR researcher, also compared the findings to AI 2027’s timeline. Ryan Greenblatt, a METR researcher formerly of AI safety organization Redwood Research and one of three external researchers permitted to investigate OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face, said he “was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026.”

Frustration is mounting over Anthropic’s approach to safety

Beyond highlighting the speed of AI development, the report has also fueled a growing sense of frustration over Anthropic’s role in driving that progress. The company has been one of the most vocal proponents of responsible AI development — and no stranger to calling for others to slow down — yet appears to be racing ahead itself. This report only builds on already heightened tensions from its IPO prospectus and future plans released last month.

Anthropic’s decision to heavily redact the report, citing grounds that revealing more could help its rivals accelerate their own development, has fueled accusations of hypocrisy. Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher who now runs the AI Futures Project, which published AI 2027, accused Anthropic of “recklessly gambling with our lives,” adding that “it is pretty rich” of the company to cite others going faster as a reason to redact information when it does “not appear to be slowing down much at all.”

Anthropic declined to answer The Verge’s questions about the report and ensuing criticism, instead directing us to McCandlish’s post.

The redactions have also renewed calls for greater transparency and independent oversight of frontier AI labs, which grew to new heights earlier this year following a spate of incidents involving rogue AI agents. Brianna Rosen, research director for frontier security at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, told The Verge that it was concerning that companies, not governments, were effectively calling the shots on automating AI research. “For democratic oversight to work, independent evaluators need the freedom to explain why they reached their conclusions, governments need to assess the evidence themselves, and the public has to trust this process,” Rosen said. “The report was not sufficiently transparent about the evidence.”

Pressure is building for more transparency from AI labs

Hobbhahn echoed Rosen’s concerns, saying that much of the reaction to the report stems from the apparent gap between Anthropic’s public safety stance and its actions. He pointed to the company’s decision to cancel part of the assessment designed to evaluate how much compute it allocates to safety work versus improving capabilities. METR said the company said “this was due to wanting to keep the engagement focused on risk assessment for the time being, and that it would revisit compute allocation verification later on.”

For Hobbhahn, the episode underscores the need for independent safety researchers to be embedded more deeply within AI labs, with significant access to internal systems and evidence. While his organization stands to benefit from such arrangements — Apollo is taking steps toward becoming an embedded evaluator at frontier labs — he is far from alone in calling for stronger oversight of AI development.

Others have called for more direct action. In a direct response to the report, New York state Assemblyman Alex Bores, a key figure shaping the Democrats’ AI agenda, called on Congress to “ban RSI, this year if possible.” With the blue wave of Democrats — many of whom campaigned against AI companies — taking office soon, the prospect of tougher restrictions is a very real possibility.

And with AI research showing little sign of slowing down, the pressure is set to intensify. Hobbhahn said he had another takeaway from the report, too: “Brace for craziness,” he said. “It is going to go very fast,” likely way too fast for society or politics to keep up.

title: Will AI make life less meaningful? A survey finds optimism hinges on whether humans keep control.

content_html:
OpenAI recently announced that its latest artificial intelligence model had solved, in a matter of weeks, more than 100 math problems that humans had worked on for years. The news sparked what seemed like an existential crisis among mathematicians, leaving some to wonder what role humans would have in the future of their field. It’s not just academics who are worried. In a new national survey, we found that Americans are more likely to see AI as a threat to meaning than as a resource that supports it. But that view depends on whether people think of AI as a tool that will remain under human control or as something that will become autonomous.

Discussions about AI tend to focus on its practical costs and benefits, from job loss and cyberattacks to scientific and medical breakthroughs. Far less attention has been paid to its potential psychological effects, especially on our sense of meaning.

Humans are a distinctly existential species. We don’t just strive for survival but also for significance, and people who perceive their lives as meaningful tend to be more psychologically healthy and resilient. A strong sense of meaning also promotes physical health and longevity, goal achievement, financial success, and prosocial behavior. 

This is because meaning is ultimately a self-regulatory and motivational resource. When we believe our lives matter, we have a reason to make the daily decisions and pursue the long-term ambitions that keep us healthy, productive, and connected to others.

Much of what makes life meaningful comes from our relationships, work, and creative pursuits. AI is increasingly involved in all of these human endeavors. It writes code, creates art, and solves complex intellectual problems. People are even turning to it for the kind of conversation and counsel they once sought from other humans. As AI takes on a bigger role in these parts of life, how will it affect our sense of meaning?

As part of a new research initiative on AI and the good life, our team at the Archbridge Institute’s Human Flourishing Lab surveyed over 2,000 Americans to explore this question. Specifically, we presented them with two views on how AI will affect meaning and asked which one they agree with most. In one, AI supports meaning by helping individuals put more of themselves into their relationships, work, and other purpose-driven pursuits. In the other, AI undermines meaning by doing more of people’s thinking and deciding for them, leading them to put less of themselves into these pursuits. In other words, we wanted to determine whether Americans are more inclined to view AI as supporting or undermining human meaning-making.

Americans are more likely to view AI as undermining meaning (56%) than supporting it (44%). Women and older adults were especially likely to hold this view of AI as a threat to meaning. Meanwhile, men and younger Americans were more evenly divided.

We also suspected that people’s attitudes about how AI will affect meaning would be connected to how they conceptualize AI. There is an active debate about what kind of technology AI is. Some think of it as a powerful but normal technology, like electricity or the internet, that will remain a tool humans direct and control. Others, including some of the people building AI, believe it is a fundamentally different technology — one on a path to becoming self-directed or autonomous.

We asked Americans which view they agree with most, and they are almost evenly split. Forty-eight percent see AI as a normal, human-directed technology, while 52% see it as a fundamentally new technology that will become autonomous.

Why would these views be connected to meaning? Ultimately, people find their lives most meaningful when they believe that they matter, that their efforts make a difference in the world. If people think of AI as a tool that humans control, like past technologies, they may view it as something that can help them make a difference, even if it disrupts how they live and work. But if they imagine it as fundamentally new because it could become autonomous, they may worry that humans will no longer be the primary agents in the world, making their contributions less significant

As predicted, how people conceptualize AI is strongly related to how they think it will affect meaning. Among Americans who envision AI as human-directed, 63% believe it will support people’s ability to live meaningful lives, and 37% believe it will undermine it. Among those who expect AI to be autonomous, the pattern flips. Just 27% believe AI will support meaning, and 73% believe it will undermine it. This relationship held across every demographic group we examined, and it was larger than any of the demographic differences we observed.

As we grapple with existential concerns about AI, it is worth remembering that technological innovation has always disrupted economic and cultural life, and it has likely challenged people’s sense of meaning along the way. But humans adapted. We are an agentic, creative, and resilient species. The same ingenuity that made AI possible can help us find new ways to make significant contributions to the world. And regardless of what this technology becomes, we will still decide how much of ourselves we put into the people, projects, and pursuits that make life meaningful.

title: Ambiguity or clarity?
summary: This is a choice we rarely name. Putting effort into how much ambiguity we can handle can define a career and give us a path forward in our social and cultural interactions as well. Our desire for clarity is based on safety and how we think about risk. If you know exactly what to expect, […]
reason: Seth Godin on choosing ambiguity over clarity, a useful frame for a PM lead.
content_html:
This is a choice we rarely name.

Putting effort into how much ambiguity we can handle can define a career and give us a path forward in our social and cultural interactions as well.

Our desire for clarity is based on safety and how we think about risk. If you know exactly what to expect, you won’t be held responsible for things that feel like they’re out of your control.

Clarity pushes us to put things in a category, a predictable box, well-labeled.

Ambiguity, on the other hand, is the nature of the future. All interactions with other people, with complex systems and with what hasn’t happened yet are somewhat unpredictable.

That range of outcomes is where possibility lies.

“I’m not sure.”

“This might not work.”

“We’ll be okay.”

Pretending that the ambiguous is certain is a short-term sort of bravado that works in the movies and politics but not in real life.

For the rest of us, there’s the chance to embrace the soft edges of ‘perhaps’ on our way to make things better.

HT to Seth B.

The free version of the app allows you to manually adjust the brightness level of the Apple logo, independent of the MacBook Pro's display brightness level. You can also turn it off entirely with a single click, rather than having to use Terminal.

Another free option is a "Breathe" mode that makes the logo's light gently pulse similarly to the sleep indicator light on older MacBooks.

A one-time payment unlocks the Pro version of the app: $9 for a limited time or $15 later. here's what it can do:

- manually set logo brightness (apple doesn't let you)
- breathe slowly, like the old mac sleep light
- pulse to your music
- blink when claude needs you
- turn the logo light off with one click

try it here: https://t.co/WZTWMq5yAf https://t.co/FI0o9ayKBZ

— juan (@juanbuis) November 6, 2026


Apple began phasing out the glowing logo on MacBooks in 2015, but it brought back the feature with the new 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models with PROLED XDR displays released on Friday. On older MacBooks, the logo was illuminated by the display's backlight, but OLED displays do not have a backlight, so a new method was required.

Daring Fireball's John Gruber was told that Apple engineered a "custom light source just to enable the logo to glow once again, without adding any additional thickness to the lid." Why? "Because it's awesome," he heard an Apple representative say.

By default, Apple says the logo is illuminated whenever the Mac is awake. It automatically brightens or dims based on the screen's brightness level and your environment's lighting conditions detected by the computer's ambient light sensor.

Buis said the logo is lit by a white LED that does not change colors.

title: The US let Nvidia sell chips to an empty office in China
summary: Concerns are being raised that neither the Commerce Department nor Nvidia are doing their due diligence when it comes to vetting Chinese firms cleared to handle the company's H200 AI chips. According to The New York Times, New Matrix is on the list of approved firms, yet its offices are empty, "a hollow gray shell […]
reason: Shows how weakly AI chip export controls are being vetted, timely policy news.
content_html:
Concerns are being raised that neither the Commerce Department nor Nvidia are doing their due diligence when it comes to vetting Chinese firms cleared to handle the company’s H200 AI chips. According to The New York Times, New Matrix is on the list of approved firms, yet its offices are empty, “a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling where lights should be.” In fact, the paper could find little evidence that the company exists in any meaningful way:

The US let Nvidia sell chips to an empty office in China

The government is approving sales of Nvidia’s AI chips to Chinese firms with ties to blacklisted companies.

Only scant information can be found online about New Matrix, which was created 17 months ago. At the building that New Matrix lists as its address, a company directory does not include the firm. At the nearby property management agency for the industrial park, a receptionist and a manager both said they had no record of the company.

What little information can be found about New Matrix is concerning. Its owners have ties to a Chinese private equity firm that has been blacklisted by the US government since 2024. And according to the Times, this is not a rare lapse in oversight, but a troubling pattern of companies connected to entities with national-security-related trade restrictions being approved to purchase Nvidia chips.

Nvidia had been restricted from selling chips to China during the Biden presidency. But the Trump administration relaxed those limits after Nvidia agreed to give the government a 15-percent cut of all sales. The company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, also launched an intense lobbying campaign and was apparently targeted by China’s Ministry of State Security in a spying plot.

title: Norris on Brazil pole as Russell rages at Mercedes over aborted lap
summary: Lando Norris snatched a stunning Brazilian Grand Prix pole position at Interlagos in torrential rain, as George Russell felt Mercedes robbed him of a chance to finish first
reason: Norris takes a stunning wet pole at Interlagos, the big F1 result of the weekend.
content_html:
Norris on Brazil pole as Russell rages at Mercedes over aborted lap

Lando Norris snatched a stunning Brazilian Grand Prix pole position at Interlagos in torrential rain, as George Russell felt Mercedes robbed him of a chance to finish first, despite a five-place grid penalty rendering that effectively irrelevant anyway.

After rain delayed the start of F1 qualifying by an hour and 25 minutes, Q1 got underway and you could tell conditions were treacherous merely by the rarely used wet weather tyres being bolted onto all of the cars, while by the time Q3 rolled around it was dry enough for intermediates.

But, and it was a big but, the weather radar suggested there would only be time for one flying lap before more heavy rain arrived early in Q3.

In the end there was time for two laps, and Russell was fastest with the first, and then looked good enough to be quickest in the second before backing off at the end of his second lap when he caught Alex Albon's Williams.

Russell's Mercedes radio exchange

George Russell: "Move, Albono!"
Merc: “So, we will get one more lap here.”
Russell: “You need to tell me mate what I'm doing, if I'm backing or going.”
Merc: “We can back up now, back up now.”
Russell: “Are you sure?”
Merc: “It’s raining heavier now.”
[Russell prepares to start final lap]
Merc: “It's raining heavily now in the pitlane.”
Russell: “Mate I should have f***ing finished the lap!”
[Halfway round lap when it's clear it's done]
Russell: “MATE! You f***ing told me to back off. What the hell!”
Toto Wolff: “George, you're P2"
Russell: “Yeah but…P2. I don't want to be P2, I want to be P1. That was a P1 lap. F***ing hell!”

The final gap was 0.204s, but it doesn't really matter as Russell will drop back five places for an engine penalty.

Norris has to be happy with a wet pole at Interlagos, a huge badge of honour for any driver and a reminder of his talent as the outgoing world champion.

The champion elect, Kimi Antonelli, took third, ahead of Charles Leclerc's Ferrari - facing a 10-place grid penalty - and two of the stars of qualifying, Liam Lawson and Nico Hulkenberg who will start third and fourth after penalties.

Lawson was the fastest initially on the inters in Q2, and delivered again in Q3 to take fifth for Racing Bulls. Will that be enough to sway a decision from Racing Bulls on keeping him in F1 next year?

Hulkenberg was also spectacular and took sixth - rising to fourth on the grid after penalties are applied, which will be Audi's highest start - ahead of Isack Hadjar's Red Bull.

Ollie Bearman and Fernando Alonso - his best start for Aston Martin this year - both impressed across qualifying to take eighth and ninth respectively, ahead of Alex Albon, who made Q3 for Williams.

Hamilton and Verstappen out early

Q2 produced plenty of drama as Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen went out, while rookie Rafael Camara crashed.

Verstappen cleverly decided not to run in the session at all to save tyres for tomorrow's race and protect his car, owing to the back-of-the-grid penalty he'll serve tomorrow for an unscheduled engine change.

He had been third quickest in Q1.

Hamilton did elect to run, but didn't switch to intermediates with six minutes to go like the rest of the field and sat in the pits in his Ferrari, basically surrendering the rest of the session for the same reasons as Verstappen, as Hamilton will also start at the back of the grid after an engine change.

Camara's red flag effectively ended Q2 early. He locked up and went straight on at Juncao - a problem corner all session - and hit the barriers.

He had also had a scrape in Q1 when he lost the car in a striaght line aquaplaning into the barrier on the Reta Oposta straight!

But Camara went from zero to hero by beating team-mate Ollie Bearman in Q1 - who also went off at Juncao late on in that session - and then took 13th in Q2 on his F1 debut.

Just behind Hamilton was Oscar Piastri's McLaren, while Arvid Lindblad's Racing Bulls (which broke down on track) and Carlos Sainz's Williams were the other cars eliminated in Q2.

Alpine's Q1 disaster

Despite the appalling conditions it was a relatively predictable Q1 exit list, apart from the two Alpines of Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto.

Colapinto reported his tyres were done on the last lap and he then appeared to hold up Gasly behind, consigning both to a Q1 exit in that order.

Despite Alonso regularly challenging towards the top and ending Q1 in eighth, Lance Stroll was only 19th via an early off at Juncao, ahead of Valtteri Bottas who was nearly seven tenths ahead of team-mate Sergio Perez, but Perez does have a grid penalty that will send him to the back of the grid.

Gabriel Bortoleto anchored the order as he went off at Juncao and broke his rear wing, ending his session early.

content_html:
Yesterday, a strong front, associated with strong winds gusting to 40 mph or more, moved through the region, resulting in numerous power outages.

As I will describe below, numerical weather models predicted this event with great skill, something we could not have done 20 years ago.   

This is a triumph of modern weather prediction technology.

Let me demonstrate this to you.  

Below is the radar image around 4 PM Saturday, based on the radar observations from the Langley Hill radar near Hoquium.  An intense radar return was apparent offshore (the thin yellow and red line, indicated by the red arrow).   This is the front.

Fronts associated with a narrow, cold frontal rainband were first described by  UW researchers, such as Professor Peter Hobbs and associates.

Even more impressive is a video of the cold front approaching the coast (from a wonderful phone app called RadarScope).



Here is a forecast of a simulated radar image, made 24 hours (from 4 PM) before the event is shown below.  It was made by the UW WRF model run by my group.  

Almost perfect.  Very strong simulated front.



A closer-in view is below.



A forecast made 60 hr before the event was virtually the same.  Strong front in the same location

A forecast made on Thursday evening, showing the strongest near-surface wind gusts, indicating strong winds over the region.  Strong enough to worry about.


The winds for Seattle made for Seattle City Light as part of the UW WindWatch system were clearly accurate, showing the threat of strong wind (the black dots are the strongest observed with the city; the gray and colored lines indicate model forecasts)


The models were very, very clear.  

There was a prediction of 30-45 mph winds over the city.  And that means power outages, particularly early in the storm season.

Such an emphatic forecast by the models was the reason I blogged about it on Friday, making it clear that some would lose power.

In fact, over 100,000 customers lost power over western Washington last night (see below).


And over 46,000 customers in Seattle lost their lights.


This kind of skillful forecasting occurs time and time again, based on highly skillful weather model forecasts.

Another reminder that it is no longer appropriate to make fun of forecasters and weather models.   😀

No longer appropriate

title: Are you really who you think you are?
summary: Who are you? You might think you know, but science offers a more complicated answer. In fact, Lisa Feldman Barrett, PhD, a University Distinguished Professor of Psychology at Northeastern University, says the inquiry may be unanswerable. A question that can be answered: Who are you in a given moment? Take, for example, someone who has a habit of interrupting while others are talking. reason: Lisa Feldman Barrett on how science complicates the idea of the self.
content_html:
Who are you? 

You might think you know, but science offers a more complicated answer. In fact, Lisa Feldman Barrett, PhD, a University Distinguished Professor of Psychology at Northeastern University, says the inquiry may be unanswerable. 

A question that can be answered: Who are you in a given moment? 

Take, for  example, someone who has a habit of interrupting while others are talking. They may see themselves as engaged — so enthusiastic that they’re compelled to interject with what they think the speaker is about to say.

The person being interrupted, meanwhile, may experience their conversation partner as rude.

So, do the interrupter’s intentions matter more than how they’re perceived?

According to Barrett, no. The perception of rudeness is just as real — not because it matters more than the interrupter’s intentions, but because it matters just as much.

“The characteristics or traits that we think are inherent to a person are not inherent to that person,” she says. “They exist to describe that person in relation to other conditions.” 

Your personality isn’t as fixed as it feels 

So, if traits are relational, then what does that mean for who we are?

We often assume characteristics such as being introverted or extroverted are immovable parts of a person. According to relational realism, however, we aren’t the sole authors of our identities.

Context matters. 

You may be extroverted when you’re interacting with people you know and you’re well-rested. You may not be so extroverted, however, when you’re in a room full of strangers and you’re hungry.

“What describes you — who you are — is highly situated,” Barrett says. “As a person, that feels inherently wrong to me. But as a scientist, it seems right.” 

This idea violates the subjective sense many of us have that we’re made up of enduring characteristics that describe us no matter where we are and who we’re with. Science, Barrett says, doesn’t bear this out.

Other people help shape who you are

The human brain contains a set of patterns, and based on the statistics of the past, it begins to make an action plan for the next moment. Barrett refers to this as “meaning making.” It happens predictively and largely outside of our awareness.

“Everything you do is an act of meaning making,” she says. “Even asking the question, ‘Who am I?’ and creating a story is an act of meaning making.”

This process of meaning making is your Perception Box, but it doesn’t have fixed walls. Instead, it consists of a constantly fluctuating set of signals your brain uses to make sense of what’s happening in your body and the world around you.

And if “who we are” emerges in part from those interactions, that means other people help shape who we are — just as we help shape them.

“The logical thing to carry away here is that we have more responsibility for the identities of other people than we might think,” Barrett says. “And the people who we interact with have more influence over who we are in a moment than we might like.”

Thus, one way to have more control over who we are is to take deliberate responsibility for who we interact with, and how we interact with them.

When her daughter went to college, Barrett offered her this advice: Seek out people who allow you to be the best version of yourself. 

“Find the people who help you to be that person,” she said. “That’s the message.”

We interviewed Lisa Feldman Barrett for Relational Realism, a Big Think interview series created in partnership with Unlikely Collaborators. As a creative non-profit organization, they’re on a mission to help people challenge their perceptions and expand their thinking. Often that growth can start with just a single unlikely question that makes you rethink your convictions and adjust your vantage point. Watch the fourth and final episode above, and visit Perception Box to see more in this series.

content_html:
Scaling security reviews at 1Password: Adding an agentic pipeline stage (safely)

In our first blog post, we introduced SAGE, our AI-assisted security code reviewer. In our second post, SuperSAGE (SAGE v2) gained context through scaffolding and consistency via the Go harness, so it could reason about the code around the diffs it reviews. The result? SAGE understands the 1Password codebase.

SAGE was a great tool that was saving our engineers time. It was also missing a fundamental element: the ability to learn from its mistakes. Thankfully, we’d planned ahead.

Earlier in the SAGE build process, we’d quietly implemented feedback collection. In short, after each pull request closes, SAGE gathers the thumbs-up and thumbs-down reactions our Product Security reviewers left on its findings, plus any comments they left on lines it didn't flag (potential false negatives). A dashboard shows which rules are earning which reactions, and how many findings SAGE may have missed.

That dashboard revealed important information. About two-thirds of the reactions on SAGE's findings were thumbs-down. Now, as we explained in the first post in this series, the Finder stage of SAGE’s pipeline is intentionally noisy; the Critic and Judge stages make things more precise. But too much noise was getting through. Every false positive that reached a human reviewer eroded a little of their trust and patience, which don’t refresh nightly the way the scaffolding does.

We also discovered a small subset of rules were earning a large share of the thumbs-down. Take one of our access control rules, for example. Every reaction to its findings was a thumbs-down, so we assumed something was wrong with the rule itself. But those thumbs down told us that a finding was wrong, not why. For that particular rule, the why could have been one of three things:

  • It was firing on code it was never meant to cover, so we’d need to narrow where it applies.

  • It was worded so broadly the Finder applied it too eagerly, so we’d need to reword it.

  • It was flagging something that isn’t really a security problem, so we’d need to retire it.

Three different problems with three different solutions. But on the dashboard, they all looked the same. We’d built something that measured the problem, and nothing that pointed us toward a fix.

So we went through every finding our reviewers had rejected across all our rules to determine what had gone wrong. It turned out the most common answer, accounting for about a third of all rejections, wasn’t a rule problem at all. SAGE had identified something real, but the code was already protected.

Say, for example, a PR adds a function that looks up an item by ID without checking whether the user has access to it. SAGE would flag this and, in isolation, it’s correct. But every route that calls that function goes through middleware that has already checked the user’s permissions. The protection is very real but it lives in a different file, so there’s nothing for an engineer to fix.

The scaffolding summarizes the code around every change, so SAGE knows a permissions check exists nearby. But SAGE doesn’t know whether that check runs before the flagged code. A human reviewer can determine that in seconds by opening the calling file, spotting the middleware, and moving on. SAGE could only read what it was handed.

Before SAGE could learn from its mistakes, it had to be able to catch them. And that meant giving it agency to look for itself.

The Prover: Giving the pipeline agency

SAGE v3, or, as we’ve dubbed it, HyperSAGE, adds a fourth pipeline stage after the Judge: the Prover.

A quick refresher on the pipeline: The Finder casts a wide net, the Critic argues against each finding, and the Judge makes a call.

The Prover is a separate AI agent that checks every finding that survives the Judge. It explores the codebase to investigate each claim. It opens files, searches, and follows calls into subsequent files, making those same moves a human reviewer would make.

If you recall our first post, the Critic stage already looks for protections, but only in the code it’s handed. The Prover has the agency to find much more.

If you’ve read the news in the past six months, you know that introducing an agentic pipeline stage meant giving it strict guardrails. The Prover has access to the entire repository within a read-only sandbox and can’t change a line or post a word. It works within a fixed token budget per finding, and we’ve granted it only specific tool actions: reading files, searching, listing directories, and finding files.

Our Prover also has a strict burden of proof. To suppress a finding, it has to do two things: cite evidence that points to real code, and explain why the finding doesn't hold up. It can't just explain in its own words, either. It has to pick from a short list of reasons — the same kinds we found when we went through all those rejected findings by hand: the code is already protected, the finding misreads what the code does, the risk is real but negligible, and so on.

That last one deserves elaboration, because every other reason on our list means the finding was wrong. This one means the finding was right, but there’s very little at stake. That’s a risk decision, so we set a very high bar. The Prover can’t just claim the risk is minimal. It has to point to the code that proves it. If it suppresses a real flaw this way, it automatically fails our test (more on that later).

If the Prover can’t satisfy both criteria to suppress a finding, it posts it to the PR as usual. So, when in doubt, SAGE speaks up.

That list of reasons was the first thing we taught SAGE. Now, when it suppresses a finding, it tells us what went wrong, which is exactly what our dashboard couldn't do.

After many rounds of evaluations to get our models and prompts just right, we turned on the Prover for the PRs SAGE was already reviewing in our two largest repositories.

As we said in our last post, a reviewer that can’t separate real findings from false positives is a liability on every PR. But with the Prover in place, we felt comfortable rolling out SAGE to every PR in those two repos. So, about 10 days later, we did. The Prover fails open, so anything it couldn’t disprove still reached the PR. And it records every finding it suppresses, so nothing it threw out was gone for good.

We gave the Prover one month to, well, prove itself (sorry). The numbers were impressive. It suppressed nearly nine in 10 findings, and nearly six in 10 of those suppressions said the code was already protected. This time, we could see where and how.

But we still had to make an incredibly important distinction. Was SAGE learning which findings matter or just learning to keep quiet?

We put it to the test.

Pop quiz: Checking the checker

Grading the Prover in production wasn’t an option (yet). A suppressed finding never reaches anyone, so no one can respond. Perhaps more importantly, if the Prover suppressed a real problem, nobody would know.

We tested the Prover using a set of past findings we’d already properly graded against one pretty simple question: Was it a real problem (true positive) or false alarm (false positive)? This evaluation set let us replay every finding through the Prover to check its work. But it took two attempts to get it right.

For attempt one, we let Product Security reactions answer our question. A thumbs-up meant a real problem; thumbs-down meant a false alarm. But we ran into the same issue the dashboard presented, which was built on those same reactions. A reaction signaled something was wrong, but it wasn’t reliable enough to make a decision. We discovered:

  • A thumbs-up often meant “useful” rather than “correct.” Some came with a reply saying the code was actually fine, others flagged something the team had already reviewed and signed off on.

  • A thumbs-down didn’t always mean wrong. Sometimes a finding was technically accurate, but another protection in the code already handled the risk, so nothing needed fixing.

  • Many findings never got a reaction. An evaluation set built from reactions stayed small, leaving many findings unanswered.

  • During Product Security review calls, one person reacts for the whole group. A single thumb (in either direction) can stand for an entire nuanced discussion.

For attempt two, we decided each answer based on something more concrete: what engineers did. And every answer required evidence to back it up.

We deemed a finding a true positive only if an engineer fixed the code before merging because SAGE flagged it. Proof of that “because” was a reply or commit message tying the fix to the finding (like “Addressed in…”).

We counted a finding as a false positive only if nobody changed the code and someone explained why it was wrong (for a reason the code supported). We checked that part, too. Most of those explanations came from the PR’s author, and authors tend to be very passionate about their code.

Then we double-checked every answer. Two AI reviewers judged each finding separately. One argued like an attacker, the other like a defender, and neither saw the reactions or the fix. When they disagreed, a third reviewer settled it.

Yes, that’s AI checking its own homework. But the reviewers weren’t the source of the answers, our engineers’ actions were. The reviewers were there to catch any answer the evidence didn’t support.

And not every question on the test carried the same weight. We made two automatic fails for the Prover: suppressing a real flaw with nothing protecting it, or keeping a finding the code being reviewed already disproves. If it made either mistake once, it failed the entire test, no matter how well it did on the other questions.

The finished test has 125 questions. The answer key is 39 true positives and 86 false positives. Only four of those true positives are real flaws with nothing else protecting them. The other 35 are hardening: real observations about the code, but for risks something else already covered, like a check further up the call chain or a guarantee from the surrounding design. And 20 of the false positives are disproved by the very code SAGE was reviewing. We also saved exactly what SAGE saw for every question, so we can replay the test any time we change a model, prompt, or anything else we want to benchmark against.

The results: Proving its worth

So, how did our Prover do on the test? The live version suppressed 85 of 86 false positives, including all 20 the code under review disproved. It kept all four of the real, unprotected flaws.1 And more than nine in 10 of the findings it let through were real.

But one number warrants a closer look: the 39 true positives — the findings engineers fixed because SAGE flagged them. The Prover kept only 13. It suppressed the other 26.

That probably sounds alarming, but all 26 were hardening findings. The Prover dropped them because the code was already protected, which is exactly what we’d told it to do.

A finding matters when it’s a real flaw that’s not protected by anything else. Hardening absolutely still has value (defense in depth), just not on every single PR, and not at the cost of burying the findings that really count. That’s the second thing we taught SAGE: our definition of what matters.

So, we’d set out to determine whether SAGE was learning which findings matter or just learning to keep quiet. After it kept all four real, unprotected flaws and let go of what we’d told it not to worry about, we knew it was learning what matters.

SAGE isn’t perfect, of course. During the test, the Prover suppressed a few real findings for the wrong reasons. They were edge cases, but they’re the reason we keep replaying our test. And that test has already earned its keep. We experimented with newer versions of the Prover’s instructions, and none of them beat the one we have, so none shipped.

But our test only knows about findings we’ve already graded. To keep it accurate, we’re building a human-on-the-loop tool that lets Product Security engineers review the Prover’s decisions after the fact, including any findings it suppressed. Every mistake they catch will become a new question on the test.

Those reviews will also help us answer the question our dashboard couldn’t: should we narrow a misfiring rule, reword it, or retire it? Between the Prover’s reasons and Product Security’s corrections, we’ll know just what to do. So far, the Prover has been sorting through everything the (noisy) Finder flags. After we refine the rules themselves, there will be less to sort through.

Code security matters beyond our two biggest repositories, though. We built SAGE’s ruleset from their review history, so many of its rules assume code that only exists there. Getting the rules right will be how SAGE earns its place in the rest of our codebase.

SAGE learned what matters in our two largest repos. Next, it learns what matters everywhere else.

We’ll share those details in Part 4.

  1. 100% is a great score. But four is a small sample, and this is an internal test. A small sample is a good problem to have – it means real, unprotected flaws don’t come along often, thanks to our engineers – but it means we have to keep adding to the test.

title: How To Live A Good Life: 6 Secrets From Ancient Wisdom
summary: To say Michel de Montaigne had a run of bad luck would be a massive understatement. First his best friend dies, probably of the plague. Then his father passes away from a kidney stone. Then his younger brother is killed by a tennis ball. Then Montaigne’s firstborn dies at two months old, the first of […] The post How To Live A Good Life: 6 Secrets From Ancient Wisdom appeared first on Barking Up The Wrong Tree .
reason: Montaigne's lessons on living well, in the good-life vein.
content_html:
To say Michel de Montaigne had a run of bad luck would be a massive understatement.

First his best friend dies, probably of the plague. Then his father passes away from a kidney stone. Then his younger brother is killed by a tennis ball. Then Montaigne’s firstborn dies at two months old, the first of five kids he’ll bury.

No, we’re not done. Around the same time, one of his servants came thundering down a path on a giant workhorse and smashed into him. Montaigne nearly died himself.

After all this, what did he do?

He quit his job and locked himself away in a tower. (Of course he had a tower. Noblemen in the Renaissance didn’t just say, “I need space,” and go sit in a Honda Civic eating fries.)

But that didn’t work out so well either. He thought he was entering solitude. What he actually entered was himself. That’s terrifying. I’ve met myself. I do not recommend prolonged exposure.

Alone in the tower, his brain started working overtime. He couldn’t stop the flood of thoughts.

So he started writing it all down. This led him to accidentally invent the personal essay. You might even say he also invented blogging, four hundred years early, minus the pop-ups begging you to subscribe to a newsletter. (BTW, subscribe to my newsletter.)

In 1580, this guy published essays about friendship, death, conscience, education, politics, cruelty, and the limits of reason. Great. Put those on the syllabus. He also wrote about his farts, his kidney stones, his cat, and his opinions on radishes. There’s a whole passage about how male anatomy routinely ignores direct orders from management.

Montaigne became a legend by admitting he was a typical human being. He called the book Essais, which means “attempts.” (That’s also an accurate title for my twenties and my relationship history.) The book has been in print for four and a half centuries and stands as one of the most durable how-to-live manuals ever produced, written by a man whose primary qualification was admitting he had no idea how to live.

So today we’re going into the tower with him. We’re going to sit at the feet of a guy who wrote about his own gas and see what one of the all-time greats can teach us about living a good life.

We’ll be drawing on “Essays” by Michel de Montaigne and “How to Live” by Sarah Bakewell.

Let’s get to it…

 

Ask “What Do I Know?”

Que sais-je? was Montaigne’s motto. Translation: What do I know?

Montaigne wrote during the French Wars of Religion, when Catholics and Protestants were demonstrating their superior relationship with God by murdering one another in bulk. He noticed the single ingredient every killer had in common: certainty.

Nobody’s ever committed an atrocity while saying, “Honestly, I could be wrong about this.”

Hence, his motto “What do I know?” It keeps you humble and open-minded. It allows you to change your mind and apologize. And research shows this kind of intellectual humility might even make you better at predicting the future.

In a previous post we discussed Phil Tetlock’s superforecasters, those people who are able to outpredict professional intelligence analysts by ~30 percent. One of their secrets?

They stay humble. Unlike most experts, they’re willing to change their minds. They practice a statistical version of Que sais-je?

(To learn how to keep your brain sharp as you age, click here.)

So Montaigne knew the limits of his knowledge. But what about emotions?

 

Swap Bad Feelings

These days you’re told to treat every feeling like it’s some wise messenger from your deepest self. Even if it’s painful, you must sit with it, explore it, invite it in, follow its Substack.

Montaigne disagreed.

In “On Diversion,” he said: “Some painful idea gets hold of me; I find it quicker to change it than to subdue it. If I cannot substitute an opposite one for it, I can at least find a different one. Change always solaces it, dissolves it and dispels it. If I cannot fight it, I flee it.”

Harvard’s Daniel Wegner found evidence for a similar principle with the most famous polar bear in psychology. Yeah, you know this one. You tell your brain not to think of a white bear and it immediately becomes a white-bear breeding program.

But the half of Wegner nobody quotes is his finding that focused distraction does help us clear unwanted thoughts. The brain isn’t good at following “stop” orders but it’s a big fan of “look at this instead.”

When negative feelings threaten to overwhelm you, distract yourself. After the initial onslaught dies down, then you can explore them. Montaigne was prescribing top-shelf psychological advice at a time when everybody else was bleeding patients.

(To learn how to overcome negative thoughts, click here.)

But what about when the emotions pile up? When the stresses of life hit us from all sides?

 

Have A “Back Shop”

We’re always being told to give everything 100%. Montaigne had a different idea: don’t give anything all of you.

“We must reserve a back shop all our own, entirely free, in which to establish our real liberty and our principal retreat and solitude.”

This sounds selfish. But Montaigne’s not against attachment. He’s all for loving your career, your partner, your kids. What he’s saying is that we shouldn’t bind ourselves to anything so strongly that who we are entirely depends on it.

Psychologist Patricia Linville found something similar. She studied self-complexity. Jargon aside, her research says, “don’t put all your eggs in one cognitive basket.” People whose sense of self contains numerous facets are better protected against stress and depression, because a direct hit to one identity doesn’t take your entire self down.

(To learn how to be more resilient, click here.)

Will doing all this stuff allow us to become awesome and impressive?

No. Because Montaigne says that shouldn’t be your goal anyway…

 

An Ordinary Life Is The Best Life

Every commencement speech is the same. A famous person in a gown tells a few thousand hungover graduates to BE EXTRAORDINARY AND CHANGE THE WORLD.

Montaigne had every extraordinary credential his century offered and yet he wrote: “The most beautiful lives, to my mind, are those that conform to the common human pattern, with order, but without miracle and without eccentricity.”

He felt an ordinary life was the harder achievement. He located true greatness of soul “in mediocrity.”

No, he wasn’t crazy. Extraordinary experiences are rare. That’s what “extraordinary” means. So if your happiness depends on extraordinary stuff, then 99.9% of your life becomes filler.

Most of life is work, errands, calls you need to return, the person beside you on the couch. And if you can’t find happiness there, man, are you in trouble, because “there” is where you live.

Psychologist Barry Schwartz called people who always strive for the best “maximizers.” And the people who settle for “good enough” he called “satisficers.”

Schwartz tracked new graduates into the job market and, unsurprisingly, the maximizers got starting salaries ~20% higher. But they also reported more regret and less satisfaction with the jobs they fought so hard to get. The study is literally called “Doing Better but Feeling Worse.”

Trying to do better is good, but the search for the best can make it harder to enjoy what you get. Stop measuring yourself against the exceptional and live an ordinary life well.

(To learn how to find meaning in life, click here.)

And what did Montaigne have to say about just being happy?

 

Savor The Good

I would love to be the kind of person who’s “present.” I’m not. Most of us aren’t. Normal is drinking coffee without tasting it. Normal is taking a walk while piping a stranger’s opinions into your head. I am very rarely where I am. My mind is usually somewhere else.

“When I dance, I dance. When I sleep, I sleep; and when I am strolling alone through a beautiful orchard, although part of the time my thoughts are occupied by other things, for part of the time too I bring them back to the walk, to the orchard, to the delight in being alone there, and to me.”

The important word in that quote isn’t “dance.” It’s “back.” Montaigne’s mind wouldn’t stay put. He had to bring it back. It takes effort to stay in the moment.

“I ‘pass’ the time when tide and time are sticky and unpleasant: when good, I do not want to ‘pass’ time, I savour it and hold on to it.”

Pass the bad. Hold the good. There’s some solid advice for you. But we run it backwards. We get stuck on the bad. Replay the argument, re-read the passive-aggressive email. And when something good happens? We sprint through it like it’s on fire.

Killingsworth and Gilbert’s study “A Wandering Mind Is an Unhappy Mind” found that mind-wandering predicts unhappiness regardless of what people are doing. And Fred Bryant’s work on savoring showed good things feel much better when we take the time to really appreciate them.

Four hundred years before Jon Kabat-Zinn had everyone yapping about mindfulness, a guy in a tower with a urinary tract like a gravel driveway had already written everything you need to know about it.

(To learn how to stay happy, click here.)

And what about the mistakes we’ll inevitably make in this life?

 

Regret Nothing

Montaigne’s life included civil war, plague, kidney stones, and the deaths of five of his six kids. And yet he wrote: “If I had to live again, I would live as I have done; I neither regret the past nor fear the future.”

He meant it. Nobody who publishes bladder updates is running a vanity project.

Montaigne judged decisions by the thinking that produced them, not by the results that followed. A bad outcome doesn’t automatically mean you made a bad decision.

We should do the same. Your past self didn’t have the evidence your present self has. But future-you shows up, surveying your mistakes all like, “Why didn’t you see this coming?” Because I wasn’t you yet, you chronological idiot. Cool it with the time-travel bullying.

“But doesn’t regret keep me sharp?”

Nope. Researchers Breines and Chen found that treating yourself with compassion after failure increases motivation to improve.

When you blow it, extract a brief lesson. One sentence. Then close the file. That one sentence is valuable. Everything after it is just beating yourself up.

(To learn how to overcome regret, click here.)

Okay, we’ve covered a lot. Let’s round it all up and learn what the wise Monsieur Montaigne had to say about relationships…

 

Sum Up

Here’s how to live a good life…

  • Ask “What do I know?”: You’ll be less likely to start a religious war and it might even help you predict the future.
  • Swap Bad Feelings: Get rid of bad feelings by distracting yourself. We’re all excellent at distraction these days so this is basically the easiest advice ever.
  • Have A “Back Shop”: If you give everything 100%, you become the person who sighs loudly while doing things no one asked you to do, then gets mad that nobody applauded. Ask me how I know.
  • An Ordinary Life Is The Best Life: Nobody fantasizes about being extraordinarily patient with their kids, extraordinarily faithful to their spouse, extraordinarily reliable to their friends, or extraordinarily calm while waiting on hold with the insurance company. Those are all available right now. But that’s not what you meant by “extraordinary,” was it?
  • Savor The Good: The good life is right here. It’s the orchard you are currently walking through while listening to a podcast about somebody else’s orchard.
  • Regret Nothing: Judge past decisions by then-information, not now-information.

When Montaigne was in his mid-twenties, he met Étienne de La Boétie, and that was it. They almost immediately became best friends.

Four years later La Boétie died.

The guy who told us never to give anyone all of ourselves had learned it the hard way. He’d already given someone everything. And when La Boétie died, Montaigne said he felt like only half a person.

Some think Essays is actually a long letter to La Boétie. By writing to his absent friend, Montaigne ended up speaking to all of us. Every reader for 450 years who thought, “Wait, this dead French guy is describing me,” is sitting in La Boétie’s empty chair.

If you’re lucky enough to have a friend like La Boétie, don’t assume they know how much they mean to you. Don’t postpone the gratitude until some “later” when your inbox is clear and your life is tidy.

There is no tidy later.

Tonight, call and tell them. And don’t say some blog post sent you.

So, after all of Montaigne’s wisdom, what do I know?

Not much. Less than I thought. I don’t know why people leave before we’re done needing them.

But I know this. When someone cares about you like Montaigne cared about La Boétie, believe them.

The guy who doubted nearly everything didn’t doubt his friend.

The post How To Live A Good Life: 6 Secrets From Ancient Wisdom appeared first on Barking Up The Wrong Tree.

title: Restrictive design
summary: Design of any kind requires empathy. If you’re making it for yourself, it’s a hobby. Everything else is for someone else. Great designers know who it’s for. And the design is for them, not for the designer. Annie Jean-Baptiste teaches us about restrictive design. This is what happens when the designer fails to identify and […]
reason: Seth Godin on design as empathy for a specific user.
content_html:
Design of any kind requires empathy. If you’re making it for yourself, it’s a hobby. Everything else is for someone else.

Great designers know who it’s for. And the design is for them, not for the designer.

Annie Jean-Baptiste teaches us about restrictive design. This is what happens when the designer fails to identify and recognize who the work is for, and then leaves people out. “Exclusion is a business decision, even when you did not mean to make it.”

Not everything needs to be designed for everyone. But all well-designed experiences and products are designed for someone.

Name your people, invite them in and give them what they need.

title: Norris wins as Mercedes clinches title with a scrappy race
summary: Lando Norris survived a late downpour to win at Interlagos, as Mercedes sealed the constructors’ title despite its first podium-less GP of the year
reason: Norris wins a chaotic Brazilian GP as Mercedes clinches the title.
content_html:
Norris wins as Mercedes clinches title with a scrappy race

Lando Norris survived a late downpour to take McLaren’s first race win in three months at the Brazilian Grand Prix, as Mercedes sealed the Formula 1 constructors’ title despite its first podium-less GP of the year.

Norris lost the race lead almost immediately off the line as Kimi Antonelli’s Mercedes rocketed past him on the run to Turn 1, with Liam Lawson’s Racing Bulls then quickly demoting Norris to third. 

Norris soon wrestled second back from Lawson, but Antonelli escaped down the road in the lead as the field waited for the right moment to switch from intermediate to slick tyres.

McLaren and Norris got that call right as he pitted a lap before Antonelli and closed a lot of that gap. 

Antonelli struggled to fire up his soft tyres and ended up spinning at Turn 1 on his second lap, allowing Norris into the race lead. 

Antonelli’s slide continued as the Red Bulls, Isack Hadjar and Max Verstappen, picked him off.

He reported his car was steering by itself, and he was struggling to get around the left-hand corners in particular.

Norris went unthreatened thereafter, building such a solid gap out front that even a late-rain shower and switch back to intermediates didn’t do anything to unsettle his grip on the lead.

It marks Norris and McLaren’s first victory since Zandvoort in late August. 

The podium was completed by Verstappen and Hadjar, the former of whom charged from 21st on the grid, making 10 of those positions up in the first couple of laps. 

George Russell ended up beating Antonelli for the first time since Baku in September, despite spinning in the pitlane after changing from intermediates to slick tyres.

He regained some of the lost time by doing just one stint on slicks while most other drivers needed two sets before the late switch back to intermediates.

Russell then passed Antonelli despite also reporting balance issues aboard his Mercedes. A later unsafe pit release time penalty for Antonelli made no difference to his result.

Fourth and fifth is enough for Mercedes to clinch the constructors’ title - its first since 2021 - with three races to spare, as Ferrari suffered a tricky race.

Like Verstappen, Lewis Hamilton made a spirited opening lap charge, going from 20th to ninth, but he fell back as he struggled on his intermediates, even being passed by Fernando Alonso’s Aston Martin Honda.

Hamilton was the first to switch to slick tyres and regained positions there, but he lost time to a spin just before he needed to pit for intermediates again at the end of the race. 

That left him ninth at the chequered flag, while team-mate Charles Leclerc was seventh on the road before a 5s penalty for a clash with Lawson meant he dropped to eighth behind the Racing Bulls.

Oscar Piastri finished 56.4s behind McLaren team-mate Norris in sixth place. 

Nico Hulkenberg took the final point for Audi in 10th place despite having to serve a 10-second time penalty for going off the track at Turn 1 while fighting with Franco Colapinto’s Alpine.
