reason: The national security angle on Nvidia's CEO scandal, with Gruber's take on the NYT reporting.
content_html:
Maggie Haberman, Jonathan Swan, Julian E. Barnes, and Tripp Mickle, reporting for The New York Times (gift link):

Mr. Rubio’s memo was circulated to administration officials with high-level security clearances ahead of a trip Mr. Trump took to China in May, the people briefed on the matter said. They spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive material.

Despite his status as an A.I. pioneer and head of one of the world’s most valuable companies, Mr. Huang was initially left off the list of major business and tech executives invited to join Mr. Trump in China. It is unclear whether the exclusion was connected to the memo. By that point, a number of people inside the administration were concerned about Mr. Huang’s influence on the president’s policy of only lightly regulating A.I., people briefed on the matter said.

After Mr. Trump saw media coverage about Mr. Huang being absent from the delegation, the president asked him to join the trip by meeting Air Force One during a layover in Alaska. The president drafted a social media post saying that it was an honor to have “the Great Jensen Huang,” and other business leaders “journeying to the Great Country of China where I will be asking President Xi, a Leader of extraordinary distinction, to ‘open up’ China so that these brilliant people can work their magic.”

This Huang-Huang affair explains a few things that until now didn’t make sense, and Jensen Huang not being invited on that May trip to China — until Trump invited him on the fly at the Alaska layover — is one of them. Also worth noting that on multi-byline stories, The Times puts them in order of who contributed the most to the story. In this case it’s Haberman, who is closest to Trump and the White House:

Asked about Mr. Huang’s admission to his company about his affair with Ms. Huang, Mr. Trump told reporters on Sunday evening that he did not regret his own lack of action.

“No, I don’t think so,” the president said. He added that he believed Mr. Huang should stay on as Nvidia’s chief executive.

“I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it,” Mr. Trump said.

Trump, you will recall, was convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records related to his hush-money payments to porno star Stormy Daniels, who banged him and (spanked him with a magazine on which he was on the cover) at a celebrity golf tournament in Lake Tahoe in 2006. That was four months after Melania Trump, his third wife, gave birth to their son Barron. So take “he probably has an excuse for it” with a $130,000 grain of salt.

There’s a Journalism 101 adage that news stories should be written in an “upside down triangle”, with the most important information at the top and the least important at the bottom. Another little inside-baseball tidbit about The Times, however, is that The Times, rather uniquely, often buries the most interesting (but not most important) paragraph at the very end. This story ends thus:

In recent years, Megaspeed, despite having essentially a storefront office and little local footprint, purchased $2 billion worth of Nvidia’s products. Megaspeed builds data centers in Southeast Asia that rent out their computing power to Alibaba, the giant Chinese internet company. U.S. officials suspect Megaspeed has been helping smuggle restricted advanced Nvidia chips into China.

If true, this is politically damaging to both Nvidia and Huang personally, but the context is that Nvidia booked over $300 billion in revenue over the last year.

by Jason Snell

Apple starts to charge for heavy AI usage

Ryan Christoffel of 9to5 Mac has spotted a new feature in Apple’s Creator Suite:

Apple has officially launched its first take on charging for AI features via the new Logic Pro update—with more coming soon.

With Logic Pro’s latest update, if you select Logic Pro from the menu bar, then ‘Intelligence Features’ and ‘Show Usage,’ there’s an option to ‘Buy More Usage.’

It seems like for general AI usage by consumers, Apple is planning on wrapping access into iCloud+ plans. But this apparently is the approach it will use in its professional-level products. ￼

title: No, Apple isn’t using Live Listen to listen to you
summary: Live Listen is a valuable accessibility feature for people who need assistance hearing things around them. It can stream the sound from the microphone on an iPhone or iPad to Apple-compatible hearing aids, AirPods, or supported models of Beats headphones.…
reason: Snell debunks a viral privacy scare about Live Listen with a clear explanation of how it works.
content_html:
Live Listen is a valuable accessibility feature for people who need assistance hearing things around them. It can stream the sound from the microphone on an iPhone or iPad to Apple-compatible hearing aids, AirPods, or supported models of Beats headphones.1

This can be extremely useful for someone with hearing loss, or even to understand other people in a busy room, because the benefits of the iPhone’s multiple mics canceling out noise can make a muddled or incomprehensible conversation clear to hear.

Because we live in an age of conspiracy, some bozos have decided that an innocuous, well-documented feature that’s existed since 2020 (with iOS 14.3/iPadOS 14.3) somehow translates to “all the iPhones and iPads with this update, both personal and operational, are by default listening in on all conversations around them, transcribing them, and sending those transcriptions up to Apple for advertising purposes” to quote from misinformation across two posts on Bluesky.2

The impetus appears to be a setting in iOS and iPadOS at Settings: Accessibility: Audio & Video: Live Listen, called Remote Control. It would have first appeared in iOS 26/iPadOS 26, and the current panic alleges it was turned on by default in the 27 updates.

But the Remote Control feature has nothing to do with Apple grabbing your audio. It’s part of a privacy-forward, locked-down feature that extends the utilities of your devices logged into the same Apple Account.

This conspiracy appears to have started on X, the every-bad-theory app, but has spread. Sensible people I know are asking whether this is a risk. Let me break this down.

Live Listen and Remote Control

If you have trouble hearing people in crowded situations, places with echoes, or just in general, your iPhone or iPad can act like an isolating microphone—that’s Live Listen. You can only enable it if you have a supported device nearby and active. Then, you can:

  • Go to Settings: Accessibility: Audio & Video: Live Listen and tap Start Live Listen.
  • Tap the Live Listen button, which looks like a microphone, in Control Center; or the Hearing Devices button, which looks like an ear, and choose the hearing device, like AirPods.3
  • Use other pathways described in Apple’s support note.

Starting in iOS 26/iPadOS 26, enabling Live Listen lets you also turn Live Captions on. So you’re not only hearing a clearer or louder version of audio, you’re also seeing a running transcript of what it’s picking up. You can move through the entire Live Listen session in both audio and captions.

The remote control option for Live Listen, added in iOS 26/iPadOS 26, allows use of an Apple Watch paired with your iPhone or an iPhone or iPad signed in to the same Apple Account to control Live Listen on the iPhone or iPad that’s in use. That linked device can also view Live Captions in real time.

The words remote control and transcript seem to have provided a sliver of an opening in the oyster of Apple privacy for people specializing in outrage and ragebaiting to crack open the bivalve.

The seeming Patient Zero on X wrote:

Go to your iPhone settings – accessibility – audio & visual – LIVE LISTEN.
Turn off LIVE LISTEN.
It even says it keeps TRANSCRIPTS.
This is NUTS.

While he’s going through psychosomatic anaphylactic shock, let’s look at the real story—and the real risk!

Apple risks entire company on secret recording

You might remember Apple had a run-in with secret recording a while back. The company failed to disclose that some small amount of audio captured by Siri was not just sent to the cloud for processing, but listened to by human beings. Apple agreed to settle a class-action suit in 2025 for $95 million covering 2014 to 2024; the final details are still being approved.

You might also recall that two months ago, I wrote about the new watchOS 27 features Live Rewind and Siri Recap that Apple announced were coming later this year to newer Apple Watch models. At the time, I wrote, “Should your Apple Watch always be listening?” In the classic Betteridge’s Law style,4 my answer was: “No.”5 I argued that Apple should not release either feature in its current privacy-negative forms—both protect the Apple Watch owner’s privacy, but not the privacy of those they record without proper consent and notification.

So I am hardly a “rah rah Apple is never recording us, sis boom bah” cheerleader. I try to cast a gimlet eye across any such claim.

Thus do the claims fall apart.

First, Apple’s market capitalization is nearly $5 trillion as I write this. The idea that the company would risk its reputation, particularly after the earlier Siri misstep, and expose itself to massive lawsuits worldwide, plummeting sales, and the loss of trillions from its stock value for improving ad targeting is laughable.

Its ad business is estimated at under $10 billion a year; the company doesn’t break it out from service revenue, which was $123 billion in fiscal 2026 out of nearly $500 billion overall.

Second, this all feels predicated on a fundamental misunderstanding of Live Listen and its Remote Control option, with some degree of “death paneling” something innocuous to win…points? views? X bucks? Whuffie? I don’t know what the goal is.

The Remote Control function is poorly explained in the Settings app, and doesn’t even use that name in Apple’s documentation. More confusing, if you haven’t set up Live Listen, you see just a Remote Control option enabled by default, but there’s no Start Live Listen button.6 Which makes it feel more insidious.

Please speak directly into the flowerpot

With very little effort, it’s possible to determine that neither Live Listen nor Remote Control is a threat. Also, logic is available. But emotion overrides logic, and that’s why this column exists.

[Got a question for the column? You can email glenn@sixcolors.com or use /glenn in our subscriber-only Discord community.]

  1. Live Listen works with AirPods, AirPods Pro, AirPods Max, Powerbeats Pro, Beats Fit Pro, and Powerbeats Fit, with iOS 14.3/iPadOS 14.3 or later. ↩
  2. I don’t know what “operational” means. Maybe a bad translation of “for business operations” from Russian. ↩
  3. Add a control if it’s not there. ↩
  4. Of course I know Ian Betteridge. #glenning ↩
  5. I just installed iOS 27.3 beta and watchOS 27.3 beta, and turned on Siri Recap to test it. I forgot I had done so, and it captured a few conversations with my wife and summarized them (eerily well). I apologized to her, deleted the recaps, and disabled the feature for now. ↩
  6. Apple doesn’t provide an accounting of which settings are on by default. Remote Control was enabled on my iPhone, and many people who have never touched it also saw this setting enabled. ↩

title: Hackers Exploit Qubole's Trusted AWS Access to Breach Customer Accounts and Steal Data
summary: An attacker broke into AWS accounts belonging to multiple Qubole customers between October 14 and October 26 and stole stored secrets and data, cloud security company Wiz said today. The attacker used credentials for an AWS account that Qubole's platform uses to reach those customers. How the attacker got those credentials has not been disclosed. Qubole, a data lake platform owned by Idera,
reason: A supply-chain cloud breach where a vendor's trusted AWS access was used to steal customer secrets, with lessons for key management.
content_html:
An attacker broke into AWS accounts belonging to multiple Qubole customers between October 14 and October 26 and stole stored secrets and data, cloud security company Wiz said today.

The attacker used credentials for an AWS account that Qubole's platform uses to reach those customers. How the attacker got those credentials has not been disclosed.

Qubole, a data lake platform owned by Idera, operates within its customers' AWS accounts. To let it in, a customer creates an IAM role, which is an AWS identity with its own set of permissions.

The role's trust policy allows Qubole's AWS account to assume the role, granting those permissions. Each request to do this, called AssumeRole, must include a matching code from Qubole known as an External ID.

Apart from the attack, most of the roles the attacker assumed were unused, according to Wiz's researchers. But each role still trusted Qubole's account, so the attacker's requests worked.

Any organization that has connected Qubole to AWS, even one that no longer uses it, should check its CloudTrail logs from October 1 onward. The sign to look for is an AssumeRole request from the account Qubole's platform uses, 805246085872, that came from an address outside AWS.

The researchers did not say whether the credentials have since been disabled or whether the activity has stopped. Neither Qubole nor Idera had posted a statement about the attack on their websites when The Hacker News checked today.

Why the Roles Let the Attacker In

Every AssumeRole request tied to the attacker carried an External ID and was accepted, the researchers said in their technical analysis.

AWS accepts an AssumeRole request for such a role when it comes from the trusted account and includes the correct External ID. The code is not treated as a secret, and anyone with access to the role can view it, according to AWS's external ID guidance.

Sentra spotted the activity in several of its customers' environments and alerted the researchers.

In the accounts the researchers examined, the attacker looked for stored credentials. It read environment variables for Lambda functions, pulled secrets from Secrets Manager, and read values from the SSM Parameter Store.

It then ran the credentials it had found through TruffleHog to test whether they worked. These were the victims' own AWS access keys, Entra ID client secrets, and Okta client credentials.

The attacker also copied data out of S3. It retrieved data from any bucket a role could access rather than searching for specific data, and sometimes downloaded an entire bucket in a single session.

The researchers have not linked this campaign to any other publicly reported activity, and say the targeting does not match what state-backed groups usually go after.

Qubole also lets customers connect with AWS access keys instead of a role. From October 8 to October 11, an attacker used customers' own AWS access keys, which the researchers believe had been set up for Qubole.

That attacker then compromised a few of the victims' cloud environments. This activity has not been linked to the AssumeRole abuse.

How to Check Your Accounts

Wiz's hunting guidance covers CloudTrail logs from October 1 onward in every AWS account that holds a Qubole role. Look for:

  • Account: AssumeRole requests where userIdentity.accountId is 805246085872 and sourceIPAddress is not an AWS address. The researchers saw Qubole's real traffic come only from AWS.
  • IAM principal ID: AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS. Any activity from this IAM user should be investigated, because only the attacker used it in the accounts the researchers examined.
  • IAM principal ID: AIDAJYRRH5Y3A7AAJM2HW, when the source address is outside AWS. The attacker used this IAM user from October 18, but Qubole's normal traffic also uses it.
  • IP: 57.129.54[.]120 and 2001:41d0:70d[:]7800::, OVH-hosted addresses that the attacker used.
  • IP: 45.83.220[.]211, 185.209.199[.]73 and 89.37.63[.]175, which are Mullvad VPN addresses. Other VPN users share them, so a match alone is not proof.
  • Session name: role sessions that start with quiam-, such as quiam-enum.
  • User agent: TruffleHog on GetCallerIdentity calls from one of the IP addresses above. Look for the same user agent in your identity provider's sign-in logs.

For every suspicious session, review everything it did afterward, especially in Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, Lambda, and S3.

CloudTrail management events log each AssumeRole request and bucket listing, but not which S3 objects were read. That needs S3 data events or S3 server access logs. Several victims lacked the required logs, so responders could not determine which objects the attacker had read.

How to Close the Route

The researchers recommend these steps:

  • If the attacker assumed one of your Qubole roles, rotate all secrets, parameters, and Lambda environment variables that role had access to, and revoke the role's active sessions. Rotating a credential does not end sessions that were already issued.
  • Remove any Qubole role you no longer need, or take Qubole's account out of its trust policy.
  • Where Qubole supports it, swap the account-wide :root principal in the trust policy for the specific IAM principal that Qubole uses.
  • Add an aws:SourceIp or aws:SourceVpce condition that limits AssumeRole requests to the vendor's documented network ranges. In this attack, the researchers said, "a source IP condition alone would have blocked every role assumption we observed."
  • Assume others can see the External ID. It is logged in plain text in CloudTrail, and vendors and infrastructure-as-code files often store it, so do not use it as your only control. After an incident like this, change it to Qubole and use a different value for each role where possible.
  • Review what each vendor role can reach. Qubole's setup guide includes a sample S3 policy that lets the role read every bucket in the account. Vendor roles are often granted access to Lambda settings, Secrets Manager, SSM parameters, and broad S3 read permissions for convenience, according to the researchers.
  • Set alerts for AssumeRole requests from a vendor account that arrive through a VPN or a hosting company the vendor has not used before.
  • Log every account and region with an organization trail, and enable S3 data events or server access logs for buckets that store sensitive data.

title: Shorter Convergence Period
summary: Mark Gurman (tweet, 9To5Mac, MacRumors): Behind the scenes, though, Ternus has delivered a different message, knowing full well that Apple remains far behind rivals. In recent weeks, Ternus held a closed-door meeting with Craig Federighi, who became Apple’s AI czar following last year’s dismissal of its former AI leader. Desiring more and frustrated by what […]
reason: Tsai rounds up reporting on Ternus pushing Federighi to move faster on Apple's lagging AI work.
content_html:
Mark Gurman (tweet, 9To5Mac, MacRumors):

Behind the scenes, though, Ternus has delivered a different message, knowing full well that Apple remains far behind rivals. In recent weeks, Ternus held a closed-door meeting with Craig Federighi, who became Apple’s AI czar following last year’s dismissal of its former AI leader. Desiring more and frustrated by what he sees as a reluctance to embrace AI with the same urgency as competitors, Ternus pushed his software chief to accelerate the company’s road map and move quickly beyond merely making necessary improvements to Siri.

[…]

Apple is already deep into work on next year’s operating systems, Bell (iOS 28 and iPadOS 28) and Poppy (macOS 28), but has changed up its process, I’m told. Apple traditionally separates development of each year’s new OSs into three major milestones known as M1, M2 and M3. Development of each stage runs for eight weeks and is split between four weeks of coding and four weeks of convergence, meaning integrating the features into the operating system.

For this cycle, though, Apple has done things differently for the M1 milestone. Instead of the normal split between two four-week efforts, Apple engineers were tasked with six weeks of coding, exploration and feature development, and then only two weeks of convergence. Employees say they like the change, indicating that it creates more time for coming up with ideas and exploring them before needing to lock things in.

I don’t think Federighi’s problem is that he’s going too slow. Less time for integration sounds like a recipe for even more bugs.

title: If the Windows Update hot patcher checks that the function hasn’t already been patched, does that mean you can’t install two hot-patches?
summary: It knows what it did. The post If the Windows Update hot patcher checks that the function hasn’t already been patched, does that mean you can’t install two hot-patches? appeared first on The Old New Thing .
reason: Raymond Chen explains how Windows hot patching stacks multiple patches, classic Microsoft engineering detail.
content_html:
In my earlier discussion of how Windows Update uses the hot-patching space (and how nobody else should be using it), the question arose of what happens when Windows Update wants to hot-patch a binary that has already been hotpatched. Does this mean that you cannot apply hot patches two updates in a row?

Microsoft issues hot patches for two updates in a row. I linked to it in the original article, and here it is again: Hotpatch for Windows client now available.

Notice in the diagram that Windows supports two hot-patch cycles before forcing a traditional update.

 
Hot-patch
track		     Hot-patch
update		 → Hot-patch
update		       Hot-patch
update		 → Hot-patch
update		    
                   
Traditional
track		 Traditional
update		 → Traditional
update		 → Traditional
update		 → Traditional
update		 → Traditional
update		 → Traditional
update		 → Traditional
update
  Jan
baseline		   Feb   Mar   Apr
baseline		   May   Jun   Jul
baseline

The first month of each quarter issues a traditional update. Administrators who opted into the hot-patch track can install two months of hot patches, while everybody else continues to get traditional updates. At the start of the next quarter, everybody gets a traditional update again, and the cycle continues.

Okay, so how can Windows Update apply a hot-patch on top of another hot-patch?

Why can’t you tickle yourself?

Your brain knows that you’re the one doing the tickling, so it suppresses the tickle response.

And Windows Update knows that it’s patching something that it already patched, so it knows what it did to apply the hot-patch, and therefore it knows what code was originally there before it performed the hot-patch. I think all it has to do to patch a patch is update the far jump target in the trampoline to point to the new hot-patch function.

I suspect that the limit of two stacked hot-patches avoids an unbounded accumulation of internal data structures that are used to keep track of all the hot-patches, and to ensure we don’t run out of patch space in the binary itself.

content_html:
The iOS 27.2.1, iPadOS 27.2.1, and macOS 27.2.1 updates Apple released today fix a handful of security vulnerabilities. With the security fixes implemented, it's a good idea to update as soon as you can.


A bug with iMessage could let a remote attacker join a group chat to receive its messages, and another could let users see messages sent before they joined a group chat.

Most of the vulnerabilities involved AirPlay and Bluetooth. A malicious Bluetooth device could pair without user interaction, and another bug could let a nearby attacker corrupt process memory. Several bugs could allow an attacker to bypass the rate limit on ‌AirPlay‌ pairing code attempts.

Apple credits itself on four of the vulnerabilities, so they were found internally.

With the macOS update, Apple also addressed the eMudhra certificate vulnerability, adding protections for command-line tools.

Apple did not say that the flaws have been exploited in the wild, but with the details on each vulnerability now public, devices that are not running the new software could be more vulnerable to attack.

feed: MacRumors: Mac News and Rumors - All Stories
reason: Apple finally removes trust in the compromised eMudhra certificate for command-line tools, a real-world PKI cleanup story.
content_html:
The macOS Golden Gate 27.2.1 update Apple released today addresses the eMudhra certificate vulnerability, and Apple recommends users update to the latest software.


For Macs that run macOS 26 or macOS 15, Apple has released macOS 26.7.3 and macOS 15.8.3.

Apple previously blocked the compromised certificates in Safari, Mail, and apps that use Apple frameworks in October to protect most users, but command-line tools like curl and git were still able to accept them. With macOS 27.2.1, command-line tools will no longer accept the certificates.

Prior to releasing the macOS 27.2.1 update, Apple offered instructions for those who wanted to protect themselves from the compromised eMudhra certificates when using command-line tools, directing users to manually remove the affected root certificates from their Mac's "/etc/ssl/cert.pem" file.

Apple still has those instructions available for users who are unable to update their Macs.

The compromised security certificates were issued by certificate authority eMudhra. An investigation launched by Mozilla found the certificates used private key values below 256, making them trivial to recover. Attackers could use the keys to create fraudulent certificates that appeared valid for any website.

Apple also fixed the issue in the macOS Golden Gate 27.3 beta, but with the fix also included in macOS 27.2.1, users won't need to wait until December for protection.
Related Roundup: macOS Golden Gate

Anthropic is announcing two new models today: Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, which it says are designed to take on “daunting” technical challenges. The company claims the new models show improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision, and can generate outputs faster than the 5.1 versions of the Fable and Mythos models.

Anthropic launches new Claude Fable and Mythos 5.2 models

Claude Fable 5.2 is designed to take on big technical challenges, and it’s available today.

Claude Fable 5.2 is good at challenging software engineering problems, Anthropic says, and can orchestrate agent teams and tackle long-running projects. The new model has also solved some complex scientific problems, including two open theoretical physics problems.

During prerelease testing, the two models have “helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours,” Anthropic says.

Claude Fable 5.2 is launching today. As for Claude Mythos 5.2, only vetted organizations will have access to start. The new 5.2 models follow the release of Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 in September.

reason: Gruber-linked Levy profile of the exec behind Apple hardware, a rich read on where Apple is headed.
content_html:
Steven Levy at Wired, in a terrific post-event follow-up to his exclusive early look at the new MacBook Pros (News+ link):

I first met Ternus in 2015, when I spent a day with him at Apple’s Input Design Lab, a testing facility in Cupertino. He’d risen to VP for Mac, iPad, Ecosystem, and Audio Engineering, and he struck me as affable and knowledgeable. (He spent four years right out of college at a virtual reality company, but he’s been at Apple ever since.) The peg to my story at the time was how this unknown manager conducted a Javert-like investigation to fix the weird sound a redesigned mouse made when sliding on a table.

That attention to detail was a legacy of Jobs’ perfectionism, which Tim Cook sustained as the next CEO. In the decade when Ternus overlapped with Jobs, he says he had only “a handful of interactions” with the founder. “But I’ve always felt like sort of a student of Steve’s teachings,” Ternus said. “And then being able to work very closely with Tim, I’ve been very lucky.” [...]

The extent to which Ternus is a deep Apple insider became clear when I probed him on his views on being a corporate leader. I asked him which non-Apple CEOs he admires, and he was stumped. “I haven’t really thought about that,” he said. I asked whether any business books had an impact on him. “Not really,” he said. “Of course I’ve read books, but there’s so much to be learned from the people I get to work with.” Indeed, every time I tried to pin down Ternus on what mark he wants to make at Apple, he deflected the question and told me how he will continue Apple’s commitment to internal collaboration.

title: How America helped shape the man who attacked Pearl Harbor

reason: Pacific War history angle on Yamamoto, a thoughtful deep read.
content_html:
The adults in town were surprised. Isoroku Takano, later Yamamoto*, was an introverted child. At school, he usually sat quietly with his arms crossed. After school, he didn’t stop to play with the other boys, but headed straight home. Unusually, though, the boy seemed to come out of his shell when he talked to an American who had recently arrived in town. 

The man, a missionary named Horatio Newell, had left an impression, especially after he constructed the first baseball diamond in the area. Yamamoto was one of the local boys who eagerly learned the new American sport. He played hard and was once even knocked out by a thrown ball as he was trying to reach second base.

Yamamoto also joined the Sunday School classes. Newell had a knack for making the lessons engaging for little boys, at one point even pulling a live snake out of his pocket as he told them the story of the fiery serpents from the Book of Numbers. Beyond the stories of the Christian Bible, Yamamoto was also fascinated to hear stories about Benjamin Franklin, George Washington, and American ideals  like freedom and democracy.

Yamamoto’s father was supportive of his son’s interests. He was a tough ex-samurai, but he was also a scholar. He approved of his son learning more about the West and, like the other adults in town, noted that Newell was having a positive influence on the young Yamamoto’s development.

In middle school, Yamamoto obtained an English-language biography of Benjamin Franklin. He painstakingly read the book, stopping often to look in the English dictionary. In the front of the book, he scribbled Franklin in English and then scribbled kanji characters that spelled out Franklin in Japanese. He told those around him that he was inspired at how Benjamin Franklin had worked to free the colonies from the English king, and that he wanted to be like that someday.

After graduating high school, Yamamoto entered the Japanese Naval Academy. At the time, Japan was becoming increasingly nationalist — the cult surrounding the Emperor growing more fervent. Yamamoto received some abuse from older students who didn’t like that he had a Christian Bible on his desk. He simply replied that it held many valuable lessons.

In 1909, Yamamoto and his classmates were sent on a training cruise to the West Coast of the United States. Their ships stopped in Shanghai, Singapore, and Sydney, Australia, before crossing the Pacific on their way to their first destination in the U.S., the rapidly growing city of Los Angeles, California. 

Yamamoto’s initial exposure to America through Newell had given him a positive, somewhat idealized view of the country. However, relations between Japan and America had recently become strained, and the issues were well covered in the Japanese press. For example, three years earlier, San Francisco had kicked all Japanese children out of the city schools. The order had been popular, leading to further anti-Japanese laws. Two months before Yamamoto’s ship arrived in California, the state’s legislature passed a statewide ban of Japanese students, and there were another dozen anti-Japanese bills passed that year.

The two Japanese Navy ships carrying Yamamoto and his classmates arrived in Los Angeles on April 28th. Reading about the anti-Japanese sentiment in the press was one thing, but it must have been unnerving for them to meet Americans in person and face their hostility. Yamamoto sent his brother a postcard that said Los Angeles is “a fast-growing city of 300,000 that was a small town not long ago. It is extremely anti-Japanese and there is no goodwill towards us at all.”  

After a few days, the Japanese ships sailed north, crossed through the Golden Gate and docked at the port of San Francisco on May 3. Although there was abundant anti-Japanese feeling at the citizen level and in the legislature, the Japanese sailors were given a warm official welcome by the U.S. Navy. The Japanese officers attended a dinner at the Fairmont Hotel, where James Gillett, the Republican governor of California, noted that “on the other side of the Pacific there is Japan, a great world power. On this side, there is America, another world power, and there is every reason why these two governments should always maintain their friendly feelings.” 

The next morning, Yamamoto and the other young officers were treated to an outing to see the magnificent views of Mount Tamalpais, before returning to San Francisco Bay, where they were hosted to dinner parties on board the USS Tennessee, West Virginia, Pennsylvania, and California.

Despite the official niceties, Yamamoto got a full dose of the prevalent anti-Japanese sentiments. Dropping another postcard to his brother, he wrote, “San Francisco is the source of the anti-Japanese feelings in the U.S. We get an unfriendly welcome from everyone we meet, be they Americans or not.”

After leaving San Francisco, the ships sailed to Seattle and Vancouver, where they had a similar warm official welcome. On Memorial Day in the city of Tacoma, Yamamoto and other cadets marched in a parade along with U.S. military veterans, basking in the attention of 100,000 spectators. Yet, before the celebration, the police had needed to crack down on people posting “fire the Jap” on local telephone poles.

Yamamoto’s next postcard to his brother said, “The image of America is that it’s a country of freedom where you can make money. But there is another side to the story. Money rules over principles and there is no compassion.”

He spent the next decade rotating among various roles in the Japanese Navy. Destined for higher ranks, he and some of the other most promising young officers were selected to go abroad and learn more about the designated future enemy, the United States.

In the Spring of 1919, Yamamoto boarded the mail ship Suwa Maru in Yokohama, again bound for San Francisco. At the top of the gangplank, he turned and waved goodbye to the friends and family who had come to see him off. As the ship left Tokyo Bay, he and the other passengers on the deck all looked with awe at the sight of Mt Fuji in the distance. Yamamoto had met the occasional foreigner before, such as Newell, but now it felt different. Almost all the people around him on the deck were Americans.

Yamamoto had been given a two-year assignment. His orders were simple: Study English, and learn about the United States, particularly about its Navy, government, and industry.

Crossing America and arriving in Boston, he was greeted by Mrs. Clifford and Mrs. Morrow, who were running the new boarding house in Brookline where he would be living. Staying with the women and having breakfast every morning was enjoyable and good for his English. The conversations surfaced things that Yamamoto found surprising. For example, unlike typical Japanese women, they were educated, and they relied on servants to do manual work, rather than doing the cleaning themselves. 

A shock to Yamamoto was the prices. Everything cost more than in Japan, so he was happy to find some strange low-cost restaurants that had no waitresses. As he explained to his brother in a letter, these “cafeterias” were a good way to save money. Another way of saving money was to skip a meal and then go for cheap Chinese food.

In September, Yamamoto filled out the two-page application to the Harvard “special student” program. This wasn’t the same as applying to Harvard undergrad; it was a special program where foreigners could study English. He filled out the application in pencil, answering most of the questions with single sentences and leaving the optional essay blank. He purchased, for his own use, a complete works of Shakespeare and a nice leather Bible. 

He also read half a dozen biographies of great Americans; the one that moved him the most was about Abraham Lincoln. He later told one of his staff that Lincoln had been born in a small shack, “similar to many you can find in the poor parts of Japan,” and rose to be the “champion of freeing the slaves — in short, of human freedom.” Yamamoto admired that Lincoln “put faith in himself, always, even though he committed many errors. But the errors didn’t detract from his greatness, and in fact, the errors made him human, and this humanity was what made people admire and follow his leadership.”

Perhaps Yamamoto admired Lincoln because of their similarities in personality. Like Lincoln, Yamamoto was an introspective leader who was keenly aware of his own flaws and had bouts of melancholy. 

In January 1920, classes started at Harvard, and the newly promoted Commander Yamamoto showed up to the first day of English for foreign students. Being around a group of non-Americans was likely not what he wanted, so after a couple of classes, he quit. He then made some money tutoring other students in the evening.

He was able to watch the Boston Red Sox at the newly built Fenway Park, and one imagines he enjoyed watching the home team of his childhood baseball coach, Newell. A couple of other Japanese students invited Yamamoto to join them in running the Boston Marathon. The run along the Charles River was tiring but beautiful. As they approached the bridge that marks the end of the race, the other students were taken aback at how Yamamoto was able to turn on extra speed at the end and pass everyone. He also spent time in Washington doing work for the Japanese embassy.

As Yamamoto’s two-year stint in the United States came to a close, he reflected on his time there. He was impressed by the wealth and industrial strength of America, but his opinion of Americans was as low as it had been when he first visited a decade before. He found American students to be unmotivated and lazy. In the two years in the United States, much of which was on a college campus, he didn’t make a single American friend, nor did he make any American friends later in life. 

Many historians have portrayed Yamamoto as someone who understood, maybe even liked, America and Americans. But the truth is more complex. Over the course of his life, Yamamoto had a contradictory and complex set of experiences with the country he idolized in his youth. He was impressed by the sheer size and wealth of the nation. At the same time, anti-Japanese racism and America’s pursuit of cold winner-take-all capitalism pulled his feelings in the opposite direction. 

About 20 years after he returned to Japan from his American stay, he picked up his writing brush and wrote a proposal to the Navy Minister, where he put forward a plan to attack the American base at Pearl Harbor. He noted that if he could crush the country’s fleet, then perhaps the Americans would be so discouraged they would be open to a negotiated peace with Japan.

As he completed his proposal, it must have been a complex mix of emotions and experiences that set the table for his thoughts. Was he thinking of the America he idolized as a child — the America of Lincoln, Franklin, and baseball — or was thinking  of the America he disliked, a country of racism and greed? Perhaps, in the end, he was thinking of both.

* Author’s Note: Yamamoto was born Isoroku Takano in 1884. He took his better-known surname in the mid-1910s after being adopted into the Yamamoto family. For simplicity, I refer to him as Yamamoto throughout the article.

This article How America helped shape the man who attacked Pearl Harbor is featured on Big Think.

title: Apple Patches iMessage Group Chat Privacy Flaws and Bluetooth Pairing Vulnerabilities
summary: An iMessage flaw could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages, Apple said yesterday, and it released updates to fix it. The updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined. As of today, other updates released yesterday for the iPhone XS, XS Max and XR, the iPad (7th generation) and some Apple
reason: Apple patches iMessage group chat and Bluetooth flaws, directly relevant Apple security news.
content_html:
An iMessage flaw could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages, Apple said yesterday, and it released updates to fix it. The updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

As of today, other updates released yesterday for the iPhone XS, XS Max and XR, the iPad (7th generation) and some Apple Watch models do not list either fix.

The company's notes also do not say whether either flaw has been exploited, what an attacker would need, whether group members would see someone who joined this way, or whether every member must update to be protected.

The updates that fix the iMessage flaws also fix a flaw in Google's Brotli compression library. The notes do not mention any attacks using that flaw. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 27.

The flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat is tracked as CVE-2026-113961. It is an authorization issue that the updates fix through improved validation. The flaw involving earlier messages is CVE-2026-113960.

Which Updates Carry the Fixes

Each operating system version got its own update. The security advisory for iOS and iPadOS 27.2.1 describes all three flaws. The security releases list links to the notes for every update.

The iOS 18.7.12 notes and the watchOS 26.6.1 notes list other security fixes but not the iMessage or Brotli fixes.

The company does not say whether devices on those versions are affected by the three flaws. Its notes also offer no workaround for anyone who cannot update right away.

The Brotli flaw, CVE-2026-111497, is an out-of-bounds write in the library's decoder that could let malicious input corrupt memory. CISA's catalog entry for the Brotli decoder flaw names Google's Brotli as the affected product and says different products could use the component.

All nine updates fix Bluetooth and AirPlay flaws. Two could allow a malicious Bluetooth device, or an attacker within Bluetooth range, to pair with a device without user interaction. The notes do not say what a paired device could then do.

Two others could let an attacker bypass the limit on pairing code attempts, one from Bluetooth range and one from the same network. Another could let an attacker in Bluetooth range corrupt process memory.

Google News,

title: The Power and Legacy of Virginia Tech’s Mac-Based Supercomputers
summary: Casey Liss could have used these! (He didn’t.)
reason: 512 Pixels on Mac-based supercomputers, nostalgic Apple history.
content_html:
When we think about data centers today, we often picture rows of GPU-packed racks run by companies like Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Meta, and used by AI labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Much of that hardware does one of two jobs: training new models or running finished ones to answer requests from millions of people around the world.

A supercomputer is built from many of the same parts but for a different purpose. It is typically owned by a government lab or university and designed for scientific simulation, such as modeling climate, nuclear physics, or new materials. That work demands high-precision math and very fast communication between processors. Rather than serving the masses, a supercomputer is shared among researchers, whose large jobs wait in a queue and run according to a schedule.

Early examples like UNIVAC and the IBM 7030 were used by scientists working on atomic research. The Cray-1 came along in the mid-70s and accelerated such work to new levels. Each of these machines brought with it new technologies that made those breakthroughs possible. They were also fairly bespoke, built of components regular nerds could only dream about.

Over time, that changed. By the time the 1990s rolled around, companies like Cray saw their hardware being outpaced by newcomers who were packing far more processors into their products. The kicker? Those processors were much more pedestrian than the custom silicon older supercomputers were built around.

In 1998, David Bader built what he calls “the first bona fide Linux supercomputer” with off-the-shelf parts, including the Intel Pentium II.1

That brings us to 2003, and the subject of today’s article: Virginia Tech’s Mac-based supercomputers.

Bang for the Buck

As you can see from these photos, System X — pronounced “System Ten”2 — was built with 1,100 Power Mac G5s:

Photos from Virginia Tech’s Advanced Research Computing website, via the Wayback Machine.

Honestly, I could end this article right here. Look how badass this all is! I really do love the look of the Power Mac G5.

Virginia Tech built this supercomputer in the summer of 2003, with the goal of hitting 10 teraflops. Once it was up and running that fall, it ranked as the world’s third-fastest computer, and the fastest at an academic institution. You can see from this video that the G5 was chosen to hit these numbers without breaking the bank:

(This video played as part of Apple’s product introduction for the Power Mac G5 itself.)

The total cost was $5.2 million,3 a far cry from the $400 million spent to build the fastest supercomputer at the time, the Earth Simulator.

(System X also looked much cooler.)

Both Virginia Tech faculty members and students could get time on the machine free of charge, and thanks to the dual 2.0 GHz processors inside each G5, their projects could tap into vast resources easily.

On the software front, every node ran Mac OS X. The machines arrived running Mac OS X 10.2.7, with plans to move to Panther shortly after.

Each G5 came equipped with 4 GB of DDR400 RAM, a 160 GB Serial ATA hard drive, and a Mellanox InfiniBand PCI-X card, which allowed the machines to be linked to each other and to the network over high-speed cables. Notably, the Power Mac G5 didn’t support ECC memory. That would matter later.

The G5s were unboxed and installed by students and faculty:

The whole thing came together pretty quickly, according to this FAQ:

Planning began in January of 2003. Facilities planning began in April of 2003. Renovations began the first week of August and were completed on September 23, 2003. Computers, network equipment, and cables began arriving the first week of September 2003. The computers arrived in six shipments during a seven day period and were processed into the racks in less than 2 hours per shipment with no more than 30 volunteers working a shift.

Ethernet cabling (roughly 1200 connections) was done by a four man team from our internal communications and network services group and was completed in less than 14 days.

InfiniBand cabling (roughly 1700 connections) began September 13, 2003 and was completed by a team of five people in 10 days.

I was lucky to get an email about this from Sam Davies, who was a student and an Apple Campus Representative at Virginia Tech at the time. He told me:

In the summer of 2003, I was fortunate to be a part of the team working to put System X together (that was the official name, unofficially the Mac community and everyone else called it “Big Mac”).

The first 1,100 G5s off of Apple’s assembly line were unloaded from trucks, unboxed, and carried into server racks by a huge team of faculty, staff, Apple project folks, and student volunteers like me. Only one G5 tower in the batch of 1100 couldn’t be used, and that was because one of the Apple sales reps dropped it. (Those handles are sharp!)

Of course, having a bunch of tower machines stuffed into racks isn’t very space-efficient. The next year, Apple had a solution.

The Xserve G5

Here’s Apple PR, in January 2004:

Apple today introduced Xserve G5, the most powerful Xserve yet, delivering over 30 gigaflops of processing power per system, about 60 percent more than the PowerPC G4-based Xserve. Xserve G5 features the same revolutionary PowerPC G5, 64-bit processor used in Virginia Tech’s cluster of Power Mac G5s—the world’s third fastest supercomputer. With unparalleled performance and manageability in a 1U rack-mount enclosure, Xserve G5 is the perfect server for today’s UNIX-based applications.

Xserve G5 includes a new system controller with up to 8GB of PC3200 error correcting code (ECC) memory; three hot-plug Serial ATA drive modules that deliver up to 750GB of storage; optional internal hardware RAID; dual PCI-X slots, supporting 133 MHz PCI-X cards with over 1 GBps of throughput; and dual on-board Gigabit Ethernet for high-performance networking.

The press release continues:

“Xserve G5 delivers just what our customers have been asking for,” said Philip Schiller, Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Product Marketing. “With dual G5 processing power and up to 8GB of ECC memory, Xserve G5 is affordable, easy to manage and easy to cluster. Starting as low as $2,999, no one can offer better price performance in a 1U rack-mount design.”

Available with either single or dual 2.0 GHz PowerPC G5 processors, the Xserve G5 architecture is based on an execution core that features massively parallel computation for an unprecedented 215 in-flight instructions, full symmetric multi-processing, two double precision floating-point units and an optimized Velocity Engine. Xserve G5 has the industry’s fastest front side processor bus—running at up to 1.0 GHz and delivering 8 GBps per processor.

Building on the engineering feats first introduced in the Power Mac G5, Xserve G5 squeezes the incredible performance of dual PowerPC G5 processors into an ultra-thin 1U enclosure. An innovative copper heat sink design effectively removes heat from the processors while eight high-performance fans provide airflow for cooling the system. The fans are individually managed and monitored by a dedicated fan control processor; if a single fan fails the others speed up to compensate. The 1U enclosure has an array of over 30 sensors, including eight dedicated to temperature control, that continually monitor all critical system functions throughout the server.

Tech tore down the Power Mac version of System X in January 2004 and rebuilt it with Xserve G5s that summer. ECC memory was a big part of the reason. As the school put it: “We needed to upgrade the system to something with error correcting code (ECC) RAM. The Power Macs did not support it and the XServes were coming.”

The new array was made up of 1,100 dual 2.3 GHz Xserve G5 servers and six Xserve RAIDs. Those 2.3 GHz machines were custom-built by Apple for Virginia Tech; the public wouldn’t be able to buy one until January 2005. Each one had 4 GB of that sweet, sweet ECC RAM and an 80 GB Serial ATA drive.

The installation photos really show the difference between the G5 towers and G5 servers when it comes to density:

The aforementioned FAQ sheds some light on this version of System X:

The initial machine was torn down by eight people between January 14 and January 19, 2004.

The Xserve upgrade was completed by a team of Virginia Tech and Apple volunteers over a much more staggered period of time. Rack preparation and pre-cabling of Ethernet began in February and was completed by less than ten people.

Machines arrived in odd batches beginning in the middle of June 2004 and were processed into the racks by no more than 16 people working for no more than 9 hours a shift (first shipment; 304 Xserves racked in 9 hours by a 16 person team).

Final cabling was completed over a two-week period by no more than ten people working a shift. The machine was back online for benchmarking by August 1, 2004.

The new hardware pushed System X to 12.25 teraflops. The school boasted that “the upgraded version was #7 in the 2004 TOP500 list, and cost one-fifth as much as the second least-expensive system in the top 10.”

Apple boasted about it as well, profiling the machine on its website:

Virginia Tech gained international honors for building the fastest supercomputer at any academic institution in the world. And they did it using Power Mac G5s. From that milestone, Virginia Tech has moved ahead again with System X, a new cluster using 1,100 Xserve G5s.

[…]

“When we built the first supercomputer from Power Mac G5s, we proved that a radically-different communications technology could be used to create a large-scale computing platform,” says Dr. Srinidhi Varadarajan, director of the university’s Terascale Computing Facility and the system’s lead designer.

“We’re recognized for knowing how to build these terascale computing machines — and with very good price performance.

“But the measure of the facility is the kind of science it produces.”

Varadarajan later became CTO of AppAssure, a backup software company that Dell acquired in 2012. May we all be as cool as him one day:

Tech Goes Intel

By the middle of 2007, System X had slipped to 71st place on the TOP500 list, but was still serving the community in and around Tech.

In November 2008, its younger sibling System G was brought online. Firmly in the Intel era, System G was made up of 324 Mac Pros,4 each with two 4-core 2.8 GHz Intel Xeon processors (for a total of 2,592 processor cores) and 8 GB of RAM.

It debuted at #280 on the November 2008 TOP500 list with a Linpack score of 16.87 teraflops, though Virginia Tech claimed 22.8 teraflops of sustained performance.

Chris Foresman wrote about the supercomputer for Ars Technica:

Virginia Tech’s Center for High-End Computing System [sic] (CHECS) is famous for building a 1100-node, G5-based supercomputing cluster in 2003 called System X. At the time it was built, it ranked as the third fastest supercomputer in the world with a sustained performance of just over 12 teraflops. The CHECS is building a new cluster, this time using 324 Mac Pro towers, that will have a theoretical computing capacity of 29 teraflops.

The new system will not replace System X, according to CHECS Director Dr. Srinidhi Varadarajan. “Unlike System X, which is a production machine for computational science and engineering researchers, the new system is intended to be pure computer science research system,” he told Ars. The system will be used to study two main areas: power-aware software systems that can adjust performance automatically to maximize efficiency, and distributed shared memory systems that can run existing threaded code on high-performance clusters “as if they were scaled up versions of multi-core desktops.”

The article continues and explains why the Intel Xserve wasn’t chosen for the new array:

Varadarajan and his team chose Mac Pros for a few reasons. For one, Xserves are power dense, which requires a lot of cooling to prevent thermal hot spots. “System X has a hybrid liquid-air cooling system in a dedicated facility, which enables significantly better cooling without hot spots. This machine is however, housed in a conventional air cooled room,” Varadarajan told us. Also, the Mac Pro has a large number of power and temperature sensors built in, which is necessary for the power/performance research and tuning, as well as an additional full-height PCI Express 2.0 slot for use in other research projects. And, despite common wisdom to the contrary, the Mac Pros beat other systems on price. “The Mac Pros are highly competitive even against building a white box off the cheapest prices,” he added.

System G was designed to be as power-efficient as possible. Here’s a bit from an old CHECS website:

The system is the first supercomputer running over quad data rate (QDR) InfiniBand (40Gbs) interconnect technology. System G (for “green”) also has unique power-aware capabilities, with thousands of power and thermal sensors allowing CHECS researchers to design and develop algorithms and systems software that achieve high-performance with modest power requirements, and to test such systems at unprecedented scale. With a sustained (Linpack) performance of 22.8 TFlops, System G is the largest power-aware research system and one of the largest computer science systems research clusters in the world.

This VT Magazine article has more:

“It’s twice as powerful, a third the size, and uses a third of the power,” says Kirk W. Cameron, associate professor of computer science in the College of Engineering. Cameron helped build G with Srinidhi Varadarajan, associate professor of computer science and director of the Center for High-End Computing Systems.

Unlike System X, System G was created to improve system design first and foremost and to be used as a production computer second. The $1.2 million machine was built to develop new, high-performance software tools and applications with paramount efficiency.

When Cameron and Varadarajan, assisted by a team of fellow faculty members and scores of graduate students, set out to build G, they had an end-goal in mind. They wanted G to not only be fast but also environmentally friendly. Hence the “G” for green. When Cameron arrived at Virginia Tech in 2004–on the heels of X’s opening, and attracted to Tech because of X–“green computing” wasn’t even an industry catchphrase. But Cameron already was looking ahead at the need to conserve power.

He previously worked for Los Alamos National Laboratory, handling performance duties, “squeezing as much power as possible” out of the facilities’ supercomputers, he says. This was in 2002, well before the recent call to arms in green energy. G went on-line in 2008. “Now everybody says they are doing it, but we were lucky enough to have done it first,” Cameron says.

The system is stocked with advanced power-management capabilities, such as power-aware central processing units (CPUs), disks, and memory. A network of advanced power and thermal sensors runs throughout the entire system, with Cameron and Varadarajan able to track how much power each CPU unit in each Apple tower is using.

Using power caps, the system is able to run on lower steam when not in use or in partial use, as opposed to older supercomputer systems that run at full blast, needlessly using power, on a continuous basis. Temperature control is carefully monitored as to not overuse the massive air-conditioning units that keep the stacked, side-by-side computers from overheating.

“We wanted to try and find the most efficient way to use computers,” says Cameron.

While System X served researchers across the university and was eventually run by Virginia Tech’s Advanced Research Computing division, System G was a computer science research machine. It belonged to CHECS, was sponsored in part by the National Science Foundation (NSF), and was housed on the campus of VT’s Corporate Research Center.

That makes finding additional details about System G tricky. Even locating photos of the array proved futile; the ones Virginia Tech published in 2008 have vanished from the web.

That’s when Dr. Cameron answered an email I had sent him, asking about System G and, if possible, for any photos he had of the Mac Pros. He graciously replied with first-hand information about the project, including a couple of incredibly rare photos:

These are the only images of System G I have seen, and I cannot imagine how amazing this must have been in person.

They also prove yet again that guys with racks and racks of Mac hardware are just much cooler than the rest of us:

He also provided insight into how the project was designed to make it easier to capture and analyze huge amounts of data. The team captured data from the Mac Pros’ built-in temperature sensors, recorded the voltage and current going into the racks, and logged environmental data from the room itself.

All of this data was synthesized into human-readable information that helped inform their research and keep System G as efficient as possible:

The Legacies of System X & System G

Both systems are now gone, but their legacy remains. Choosing Mac hardware to build a supercomputer isn’t the status quo, but the work of Varadarajan, Cameron, and others proved it could be done, and on a budget.

System X may be the most famous Mac-based supercomputer, but it wasn’t the only one. In January 2005, Bowie State University in Maryland unveiled XSEED, a $1 million array of 224 Xserve G5s. In the same timeframe, the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign launched its Turing Xserve Cluster, made up of 640 dual-processor 2.0 GHz Xserve G5s. The University of California, Los Angeles had Dawson, which started as an array of 128 Xserve G5s.

System G’s legacy includes its focus on power usage, under the direction of Dr. Cameron. His work has centered on the power consumption of high-performance computing systems since the early 2000s. He is a founding member of SPECpower, helped create the Green500 list, and has worked to steer the supercomputer industry toward treating performance per watt as an important metric when architecting systems.

He is still a faculty member at Virginia Tech today.

My research into System X started in July, and what was going to be a simple blog post turned into something much bigger and much more special. I had no idea System G existed when I started this, and I am thrilled I could help tell its story. My thanks to everyone who helped make this article possible, including Dr. Cameron, Sam Davies, Casey Liss, Jason Snell, and others.

  1. NASA’s Beowulf project had strung together commodity PCs running Linux as early as 1994. ↩︎

  2. According to Virginia Tech, the “X” stood for the original goal of 10 teraflops of operating speed, not for Mac OS X. ↩︎

  3. That’s the figure Virginia Tech used in 2003. A later version of the school’s FAQ put the machine at $5.7 million, plus $2 million to renovate the facility that housed it. ↩︎

  4. Some Virginia Tech sources, including VT Magazine and the school’s press release, put the count at 325. In reviewing first-hand documentation of System G (more on that in a moment), I can confidently say the array was made up of 324 machines. ↩︎

content_html:
An iOS sandbox escape published on GitHub lets an app read other apps' files on iPhones running iOS 26 and 27. That puts seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk of exposure to malicious apps, Binance warned today. Apple's updates for iOS 26 and 27, released yesterday, do not list a fix.

A researcher who goes by forcequit,  in collaboration with 0xjohnny, released the escape, called worse_query, on Sunday, a day before those updates came out. Neither the exchange nor the researcher reported any attacks or thefts involving it.

The exchange told users to delete apps installed from untrusted sources, such as sideloaded or manually signed apps, and to update iOS and all their apps. No fix for the escape has been confirmed.

For anyone who suspects a breach, the exchange's security warning advises moving funds to a new wallet created on a clean device and resetting all active login sessions.

The researcher's proof-of-concept code can reach every app's data container on an iPhone, and some system folders on iOS 27. To use it, an app has to set up an App Group container.

He says the code is for developers and "isn't useful by itself." Other developers have built apps on it that people can install.

One of them is WQ Files, a file manager that developer Christoph Kolbicz built on worse_query. It reaches other apps' data without a jailbreak or a kernel exploit, and it can edit, delete and clear that data.

WQ Files installs via sideloading tools such as AltStore and SideStore, which automatically create the App Group it needs when used with an Apple ID. No one involved has said whether an app from the App Store could use worse_query.

The three versions in the exchange's warning are the ones listed as tested in the WQ Files release notes. The researcher gives a wider range.

Of these sources, only Erosion's developers list iOS 27.2.1, which came out yesterday, and none lists iOS 26.7.3. They added 27.2.1 this week in a README change with the note "pretty sure 27.2.1 is supported".

Yesterday's updates, iOS 27.2.1 and iOS 26.7.3, fixed two iMessage flaws and several Bluetooth bugs. The security notes for iOS 27.2.1 do not mention worse_query or any sandbox issues, nor do the iOS 26.7.3 notes. Apple does not disclose, discuss, or confirm security issues until it has investigated and a patch or release is available, the notes say.

In a reply on X, the researcher wrote that he had not planned to release worse_query early. He added that "Apple was stalling on responding to me and people started larping with it on here."

The exchange did not name any wallet app as exposed, and neither did the researcher nor the developers of the apps built on worse_query.

title: Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 Beats GPT-6 Cyber in Multi-Stage Cyberattack Benchmark
summary: Anthropic on Monday released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 models, which it said exhibit improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision. During pre-release training, the large language models (LLMs) helped its engineers "complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made
reason: New Anthropic models and a cyberattack benchmark, a notable AI and security release.
content_html:
Anthropic on Monday released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 models, which it said exhibit improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision.

During pre-release training, the large language models (LLMs) helped its engineers "complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours."

The artificial intelligence (AI) company said high-stakes risks arising from misalignment remain low, and claimed the models matched or performed better than Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1 on most alignment measures, resistance to misuse, honesty, and factuality.

"It was roughly an order of magnitude less likely than Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 to publish harmful content to public package registries without encouragement, though it still did so when encouraged by the simulated user," Anthropic noted in its system card.

On Irregular's CyScenarioBench, which measures whether a model can plan and execute a multi-stage cyber operation in a realistic environment, Fable 5.2 completed 76.3%  of all challenges, compared to 61.7% for Fable 5.1 and 61% for OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber.

In a pair of reports published over the last month, Irregular said Google's Gemini 4 Argon solved 12 challenges in the subset of the CyScenarioBench suite end to end, up from 5 for Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber and none for Gemini 3.1 Pro.

"On CyScenarioBench, GPT-6 Cyber completed 11 of 11 long-horizon scenarios at least once, compared with 8 of 11 for GPT-6 Astra. Its average success rate was 61%, an increase of 7 percentage points," the AI testing lab said. "On Atomic Challenges, GPT-6 Cyber solved all 22 challenges. Average success rates were 97% in vulnerability research and exploitation, 98% in network attack simulation, and 63% in evasion."

Fable 5.2 also scored 89.6% on the CVE Rediscovery benchmark, Anthropic's own internal evaluation of whether an AI model can independently rediscover known vulnerabilities given only the affected source code. The assessment includes 1,829 advisories for open-source projects published in October 2026.

Describing Claude Mythos 5.2 as its "most capable model for cybersecurity engineering," Anthropic said it can flag more vulnerabilities than prior models, while simultaneously getting better at reproducing and fixing them.

As before, the model's cyber capabilities are accessible through its Cyber Verification Program. Claude Fable 5.2 is available on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure.

The development comes as Anthropic updated Claude Security with continuous code scanning and automatic fix tracking to help security teams monitor and address vulnerabilities as code changes.

"Each finding comes with a severity rating, judged against your project's threat model, and an explanation of how an attacker could reach the vulnerable code, so teams can fix what's actually reachable first," Anthropic said.

content_html:
When an organization is struggling, it’s tempting for the boss to blame the team.

I’m not sure the evidence supports this. After all, other similar organizations are thriving–drawing from precisely the same labor pool.

Sure, it’s easier to be a coach if Michael Jordan is on your team, but it turns out that creating the conditions for commitment, learning and resilience are the boss’s job, not the people you hired to follow along.

title: Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities
summary: Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month's Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws -- including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook -- and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.
reason: Microsoft's November Patch Tuesday fixes nearly 1,100 flaws, a record-scale drop a Microsoft security PM should know about.
content_html:
Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969.

November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”

Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”

Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues applying this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.
