title: HomeView doesn’t need to be another app dispenser
summary: This may sound like an odd request coming from a guy whose to-do list includes filing a weekly App Report highlighting interesting macOS and iOS offerings, but I really hope Apple keeps a tight lid on the apps that can appear on its HomeView smart display.…
reason: Six Colors argues Apple's HomeView should be a focused home hub, not another app store.
content_html:
This may sound like an odd request coming from a guy whose to-do list includes filing a weekly App Report highlighting interesting macOS and iOS offerings, but I really hope Apple keeps a tight lid on the apps that can appear on its HomeView smart display. I’d even take that wish one step further to implore app makers not to flood the zone with HomeView-based offerings if there ever comes a day that Apple does open up development for its latest device.

This is not me hoping for less work in the future due to laziness, though Lord knows, I am that. Rather, it’s a recognition of the fact that, as showcased by Apple, the HomeView seems to serve a very specific purpose and turning it into a device that can run every app under the sun like the iPhone and iPad before it might lessen its effectiveness.

The HomeView needs to act as a hub when you need it to be and stay out of the way the rest of the time. And loading it up with too many apps might make it more difficult for the HomeView to recede into the background.

From what I’ve seen of HomeView during its October debut, Apple designed this $299 hub as a way to control your smarthome devices while also taking care of a few other tasks, whether that’s listening to music, checking out recipes, staying up to date on your messages or what have you. That’s true whether we’re talking about the table-top model with its adjustable Liquid Retina display or the version of HomeView that you mount on the wall. In either case, the guiding principle of HomeView appears to be simplicity.

What HomeView doesn’t appear to be is a device that demands to be at the center of your life, even if “hub” is part of the description. You’re already carrying around a device that keeps you constantly connected in the form of an iPhone, and when you need a big screen for more intensive work, you can turn to a Mac or even an iPad. In contrast, the HomeView seems like it’s designed for very specific purposes and not much else.

The app situation on the initial model arriving in stores on November 13 reflects that. Apple lists 15 included apps on board the HomeView, and apart from Intercom — a HomeView-specific app that lets you make audio announcements throughout the home to connected speakers — they’re going to be familiar offerings to anyone who’s used an Apple device.

There’s the Home app, of course, for controlling smart devices from a central location, and Apple includes a few other familiar faces for managing your daily life. Apps like Calendar, Reminders and Weather give you an overview of your day. Safari lets you browse the web from your HomeView, with a special mode for displaying recipes if you’ve got the device set up in a kitchen. Music and Podcasts let you stream entertainment while you’re going about your business, and you can connect to TV, Audiobooks and a handful of other options on your iPhone for additional entertainment resources. And there’s FaceTime for video chats — ideal for the HomeView since you don’t have to hold the device and talk like you would on an iPhone or iPad.

Save for a workaround for audio and video apps that support CarPlay, you can’t install apps on your HomeView. There’s also no App Store, suggesting that Apple thinks of this device as a closed shop, at least out of the gate.

Of course, the iPhone took the same approach initially. It’s hard to remember after two decades of “There’s an app for that” marketing, but the phone Steve Jobs showed off back in 2007 had 15 apps, and that was that. It took a year for Apple to open up the iPhone for third-party apps, and developers were quick to make up for lost time.

Could a similar scenario play out with the HomeView? Certainly, it’s possible. If you’re already using your home hub to look up recipes, why not add a calorie-counting or meal-planning app? You can access your daily schedule and your to-dos, so why not add your health data as well, with maybe some exercise apps thrown in for good measure? Oh, and the HomeView supports entertainment apps, you say? Well, nothing’s more entertaining than games, all the games, oh so many games.

That’s the sort of mission creep I think Apple must avoid with the HomeView. Some apps for managing your life make sense, so long as they’re consistent with the idea of a central hub that you’re checking when it’s convenient. But if you keep expanding that functionality to an ever-increasing array of apps, the HomeView becomes just another screen you wind up staring at, no different from an iPhone or iPad or what have you. And perhaps paradoxically, the need for a device like a HomeView dissipates as its functionality expands.

So my plea for the HomeView — to Apple, to app makers, to anyone who will listen really — is to think long and hard about expanding the home hub’s ability to add apps. Take it from someone who ekes out a living reviewing these sorts of things: Sometimes less is more.

content_html:
by Jason Snell

The Mac-based Virginia Tech supercomputers

Stephen Hackett has a great, in-depth history of that time Virginia Tech built one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers out of Macs—twice:

Tech tore down the Power Mac version of System X in January 2004 and rebuilt it with Xserve G5s that summer. ECC memory was a big part of the reason. As the school put it: “We needed to upgrade the system to something with error correcting code (ECC) RAM. The Power Macs did not support it and the XServes were coming.”

The new array was made up of 1,100 dual 2.3 GHz Xserve G5 servers and six Xserve RAIDs. Those 2.3 GHz machines were custom-built by Apple for Virginia Tech; the public wouldn’t be able to buy one until January 2005. Each one had 4 GB of that sweet, sweet ECC RAM and an 80 GB Serial ATA drive.

I love the extra mile Stephen went with the research on this one. Featuring some never-before-seen photos!

title: Git Patches Flaw That Lets Malicious Repositories Execute Code During Recursive Clones

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-111760, is an integer truncation in how Git handles its index. An
reason: A Git flaw let malicious repos run code during recursive clones, a supply chain risk every engineer touches.
content_html:
A flaw in Git can let a malicious repository run an attacker's code on a computer that clones it recursively, together with its submodules. The Git project fixed it this week in Git 2.56.1, with matching fixes for the 2.50 through 2.55 series in 2.50.2, 2.51.3, 2.52.1, 2.53.1, 2.54.1 and 2.55.1.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-111760, is an integer truncation in how Git handles its index. An extremely long path in a repository can pass Git's safety check, but Git then writes it to disk under a shorter name that an attacker can set to .git.

This lets an attacker replace a submodule's .git file with a symbolic link to a folder holding malicious hooks or configuration. Hooks are programs Git runs at set points, so once Git uses that folder, the attacker's code can run.

Submodules matter here because Git refuses to replace a .git folder with a symbolic link, but in a freshly cloned submodule, .git is a file.

The fixed versions, listed in the Git project's release announcement, refuse such extremely long paths before their length can be cut short.

GitHub, which ships Git in its own tools, explained the fixes in a detailed write-up. It advises installing a fixed version from your operating system or Git distributor, and updating any app that ships its own copy of Git.

The company has already applied the fixes to github.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud. For GitHub Enterprise Server, they are in versions 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9 and 3.22.4.

Fixed versions of GitHub Desktop and the GitHub Copilot app are being prepared. GitHub Codespaces and GitHub Actions will also get the fixed Git.

Git for Windows had not released a version based on Git 2.56.1 as of Tuesday at 19:09 UTC, a check of its release tags by The Hacker News found.

Until a fixed version is installed, GitHub suggests these steps, which do not replace the fixes:

  • Clone only from servers you trust.
  • Do not recursively clone repositories you do not trust.
  • Do not merge content or tags you do not trust.
  • Do not process binary patches or fast-import streams from sources you do not trust.

The Git releases also fix five other flaws:

  • CVE-2026-113408: When someone clones an empty repository over Git protocol v2, a malicious server can send a branch name that contains path traversal. With the files reference backend, a later update to that branch can then write outside Git's reference folder.
  • CVE-2026-114467: Merging a tag that carries more than two GPG signatures corrupts Git's stack memory and can cause a denial of service. Hosting services that run such merges for users may also be affected.
  • CVE-2026-114469: A binary patch that expands to a very large size can get past Git's patch size limit of about 1 GiB and crash Git with an out-of-bounds read.
  • CVE-2026-105437: A very large merge, with many conflicts and a large conflict-marker-size attribute, can make Git write past the end of a buffer that is too small, corrupting heap memory.
  • CVE-2026-114466: Three git fast-import features, rewrite-submodules-from, rewrite-submodules-to and export-pack-edges, could be used to read arbitrary files or to create files and add data to them. Git now rejects them in an input stream unless --allow-unsafe-features is set.

GitLab, which assigned CVE-2026-105437, said code-hosting servers are most likely to be targeted through git merge-tree. A server may run that command to check whether a pull or merge request can be merged.

The conflict-marker-size attribute can be set in a .gitattributes file committed to a repository. If a server reads attributes from the repository, any user who can push branches and open a pull or merge request can trigger the flaw.

As a workaround for this flaw, servers that cannot upgrade yet can add conflict-marker-size=7 to each repository's info/attributes file, or turn off those merge checks for untrusted repositories.

Google News,

That mode processes requests inside a trusted execution environment (TEE
reason: An inference engine RCE led to a real breach of AI agents and user data, a concrete lesson in AI infrastructure security.
content_html:
An attacker exploited a remote code execution flaw in SGLang, an open-source inference engine, and ran code on one of NEAR AI's inference servers last Sunday.

The attacker could also have seen requests being processed on that server that day, including requests sent in confidential mode, the company said earlier this week. That mode processes requests inside a trusted execution environment (TEE) designed to keep them private even from the company itself.

But the TEE "does not protect against a vulnerability in the software running inside the environment," the company said. SGLang runs inside the TEE, which is how the attacker could reach requests there.

That access has since been closed, but not before the attacker moved further into the company's systems.

The attacker reached an internal system behind Private Chat, a product the company had already deprecated. So far, the company has confirmed that the attacker downloaded account details for about 100 users there. These are email addresses and names, and for some accounts, plan and balance information.

The company found no sign that stored Private Chat conversations or uploaded files were accessed.

The attacker also reached 18 AI agents on an older deployment of NEAR AI Agents that did not run inside the company's TEE. From those agents, the attacker took data including chat history, settings and logs.

Two customers' NEAR AI Cloud API keys were exposed in logs. The company has revoked both.

After detecting the attack, the company revoked all active sessions and administrator credentials, replaced all agent tokens and took Private Chat offline. It also deployed a fix for the SGLang flaw on all of its inference servers, rotated its remaining credentials and completed a full forensic review, according to its incident report.

Access to its NEAR AI Cloud service has been restored. The company reported the flaw to the SGLang project. It has not identified the flaw by CVE number, named the affected SGLang versions, or said whether the project has released a fix.

The company has contacted users whose account details or agents it confirmed were accessed. Affected users heard directly from security@near.ai, with the steps that apply to them. As a precaution, the company asks users to be careful with messages about their account or balance that they did not ask for.

In a follow-up post yesterday, it said users who have not heard from it do not need to do anything. It has not said whether people whose requests passed through the affected server last Sunday were among those contacted.

In an October 15 technical write-up, Brave, the browser maker, said its Leo assistant runs chats with the GLM 5.3 Flash model inside a TEE operated by NEAR AI.

NEAR AI has not said whether the affected server handled any of those chats.

title: Open research, stronger privacy: Making Firefox users harder to fingerprint
summary: Firefox is strengthening protection against trackers that recognize you across websites, even when they don’t use cookies. The latest fingerprinting protections shipped in Firefox reduce the extractable distinguishing details, making … Read more The post Open research, stronger privacy: Making Firefox users harder to fingerprint appeared first on Mozilla Security Blog .
reason: Mozilla explains new research-backed defenses against cookieless browser fingerprinting.
content_html:
Firefox is strengthening protection against trackers that recognize you across websites, even when they don’t use cookies. The latest fingerprinting protections shipped in Firefox reduce the extractable distinguishing details, making more Firefox users look alike to tracking scripts and strengthening individuals’ privacy in everyday browsing.

These protections build on our research into browser and device fingerprinting, a technique that combines details about your browser and device to identify you across websites. We investigated which details contribute most to make users uniquely identifiable, turned those findings into practical protections for Firefox users, and shared our results openly so the wider web security and privacy community can build stronger defenses.

Our findings are documented in the research paper Large-Scale Measurement and Real-World Mitigation of Web Browser Fingerprinting in the Wild, which has been accepted for publication at Computer and Communications Security (CCS) 2026, a leading international conference on computer security and privacy. We’ve also created an easier-to-digest website and browser test suite to help explore the findings in the paper.

Cookie-less Tracking

Browser fingerprinting combines details about your browser and device, such as available fonts, screen dimensions, and graphics hardware, to build a uniquely recognizable profile. Each piece may seem ordinary, but together, they can enable trackers to single you out across websites, even without storing a cookie.

Effective fingerprinting protection starts with understanding which browser details trackers rely on most. Our research found that protecting just a handful of browser features can significantly weaken popular fingerprinting techniques. That finding enabled us to focus on Firefox’s protections where they can make the biggest difference and bring those benefits to all Firefox users.

To evaluate these techniques, we simulated the browser measurements collected by fingerprinting scripts from Fingerprint Pro, Signifyd, and Akamai and examined how their combinations distinguish users. The study used measurements collected from nearly 25 million Firefox users, with additional privacy safeguards beyond Mozilla’s existing data collection policies.

Those safeguards included OHTTP, which routed encrypted requests through a relay. The relay sees the user’s IP address but not the request contents, while Mozilla receives the contents without the user’s IP address. We also tightly limited data access and retention: individual telemetry records were deleted several months ago and only aggregate results were retained and published for open science. Our research paper explains the method, safeguards and ethical considerations in detail.

Less distinctive, more private

Our approach reduces unnecessary differences in the information Firefox exposes to websites. For example, Firefox limits the information exposed through screen resolution APIs to hide the size and position of the system taskbar or dock, preventing that desktop layout detail from contributing to a fingerprint. As another example, it can report processor counts as either 4 or 8 instead of exposing the exact count, which can make a browser more distinctive.

Our goal is to make more users’ browsers look similar to fingerprinting scripts while preserving the information websites need to function correctly, like language and timezone settings. Firefox also uses randomization to make other fingerprinting signals less useful to trackers, though the benefits of these techniques are harder to quantify and fall outside the measurements reported here.

In our evaluation, these protections (the most recent of which shipped in Firefox 145) substantially degraded the precision of fingerprinting in Firefox both by reducing the number of users with unique fingerprints and increasing the size of the groups of users that share a fingerprint.

The research also enabled us to identify why certain measurements differed between users. Addressing these differences produced more consistent outputs for image rendering, Web Audio, and mathematical operations on Android, reducing the distinguishing details available to fingerprinters.

These results show that substantial reductions in browser fingerprint uniqueness are achievable and provide meaningful progress toward stronger online privacy. These do not make fingerprinting impossible as trackers can surely adapt. But our research provides a concrete, measurable improvement in browser defenses against online tracking.

The built-in privacy protections in Firefox are complemented with capabilities and options to further strengthen the protection against online fingerprinters. Built-in and always-on Total Cookie Protection in Firefox segments stateful identifiers and prevents trackers from following you across your browsing using cookies. Firefox Relay provides you with unique email masks, preventing websites from linking your subscriptions to other sites via data brokers. And Firefox now integrates a free VPN that masks your IP address to protect against tracking and fingerprinting. Together with Firefox’s enhanced fingerprinting protections, these capabilities provide everyone a very strong foundation to take back control of their privacy online.

Research that improves everyday browsing

Privacy protections need to work on the websites people use every day. These findings allow us to prioritize changes that deliver measurable privacy benefits while keeping those websites working.

Some of Firefox’s fingerprinting protections, such as hiding the size of your taskbar or dock, are on by default in all browsing modes. Others are introduced first in Private Browsing and Strict Enhanced Tracking Protection (ETP) mode, while we work toward enabling them by default, following the same strategy we’ve used for years. To enable these additional protections in all your Firefox windows, select Strict in the Enhanced Tracking Protection settings. Follow the steps here if the “Strict” protections get in the way of any website functionality.

Want to explore browser fingerprinting yourself? Visit the research project page to try the fingerprinting test and learn more about our findings. For a closer look at what we measured and how we turned those insights into Firefox protections, explore our paper: Large-Scale Measurement and Real-World Mitigation of Web Browser Fingerprinting in the Wild.

We’ll keep strengthening Firefox’s privacy protections while continuing to work in the open. By sharing our research, our code, and what we learn, we’re shaping the web we envision: free, private, secure, and accessible to all.

reason: Apple's Claris is testing Harbor, turning Apple silicon Macs into private local AI servers.
content_html:
Apple's Claris subsidiary is testing an app called Harbor, which turns Apple silicon Macs into a private AI server.


Harbor works with a single Apple silicon Mac, but it also supports connecting multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory for larger models. Apple added RDMA over Thunderbolt 5 with macOS Tahoe 26.2, making clustering faster.

Harbor detects devices connected over Thunderbolt 5 and lets users browse for, download, and load open-weight models. It's described as an easy-to-use app with no manual configuration required.
Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory, enabling large models and higher concurrency than a single computer can handle alone.

Set up in minutes, not hours. Harbor automatically detects your devices over Thunderbolt 5 to form a cluster. Plug in, start, and you're running—no manual configuration, no command line, no infrastructure expertise required.


Download and run models directly. Browse, download, and load open-weight models from within the app. Harbor handles model management so you can focus on the work, not the setup.

Cluster for scale. Connect two or more Thunderbolt 5-capable Mac computers and Harbor pools their unified memory into a single inference resource. Run models that exceed any single computer's capacity, or serve more concurrent requests across your cluster.

Harbor is in early access and is not publicly available. There was an App Store listing, but it has now been removed.

Claris is known for its database platform FileMaker, which is aimed at businesses, so it isn't clear how Apple will market the Harbor app or whether it will be free. The sign-up page for Harbor asks for a company name, which suggests more of a business focus.

There are already well-known, free alternatives for Mac users who want to run a local AI server. Exo is an open-source tool for clustering Macs, and LM Studio is available for single-Mac use, but Apple's Harbor app appears to combine LM Studio's simple interface with clustering.
